utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. I was advised that, Mr. Robinson, you had something to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I just would like to put on the record our objection to the testimony of war correspondent witnesses absent of valid waiver of the privilege. You've already heard this issue before and decided it but since this witness falls into that category, I just wanted to place on the record our objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure you need to put that on record every time. It is a given, so to speak. It is understanding that you have a continuing objection, but the Chamber has ruled upon it. So if really necessary, I would rather recommend you put in writing instead of taking up courtroom time, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your indulgence. If the witness could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is you, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Edward Sebastian Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, as we discussed, part of your evidence in this case is going to be submitted in writing so we first need to deal with the formalities in relation to that submission. You testified in the Stakic case between the 16th and 18th of September, 2002; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You've subsequently had an opportunity to review the transcript of that testimony?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you confirm that that transcript accurately reflects your testimony at the time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly pause between questions and answers for the sake of interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you were asked today about the matters that you testified too in the Stakic case, would you provide the same information to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender the transcript 65 ter 22504.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3777, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And Your Honours leave, I'll read a summary of the witness's written evidence. In 1992, the witness was a journalist for the London based "Guardian" newspaper. During the relevant time period he covered the conflict in the former Yugoslavia. In early August, 1992, the witness was among the first group of journalists to visit the Omarska camp. This is Schedule C 20.2 and the Trnopolje camp Schedule C 20.4 which are located in the Prijedor municipality. The witness testified that the access to these detention facilities, as well as the Kula prison which he visited, was authorised by Radovan Karadzic. On the 3rd of August, 1992, the journalists met Radovan Karadzic in Pale where they were promised access to Omarska camp. That day, the journalists were taken to visit Kula prison. This is Schedule 18.2. En route from Pale to Banja Luka, the witness observed extensive damage to the town of Brcko which was deserted and damaged with shell-fire and mortar fire. On the 5th of August, 1992, the journalists were escorted by Major Milutinovic to Prijedor. The witness saw extensive damage to the houses in Kozarac. Major Milutinovic explained that 40.000 Muslims "decided to leave the area." The journalists attended a meeting with Serb officials in Prijedor and were then taken to the Omarska camp. The journalists observed some of the detainees when they were brought to the canteen for food. The witness describes the condition of some of the detainees as shocking. The journalists began to interview a number of the detainees. The witness describes that when the group of journalists tried to access the prisoners' sleeping quarters, they were told that although Radovan Karadzic had authorised a visit to the camp this authorisation had certain limitations. The journalists were subsequently taken to the Trnopolje camp. The witness described in detail the barbed wire fence and behind it a crowded group of men, many of who were in serious state of decay and skeletal. The witness testified to the conditions in the detention facilities and the treatment of the non-Serb detainees in these facilities. After visiting the Trnopolje camp, the journalists left for Belgrade. On the 7th of August, 1992, the witness's article on the visits to the camps was published. The witness also described a conversation he had with Nikola Koljevic in Belgrade after news of the detention facilities had been published. Within days of visiting the camps in Prijedor municipality, the witness visited a HOS-run camp with Serb detainees. The witness further described how later, around mid-August, he managed to join a large convoy of non-Serb inhabitants from the Sanski Most municipality who had been forcibly removed from their homes and were being transferred to Travnik. During the transfer, he witnessed mistreatment, beatings, and the looting of property. In March 1996, the witness interviewed Milomir Stakic and Milan Kovacevic in Prijedor and testified to his observations during these interviews. That completes a summary of the witness's written evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, I now have a number questions for you. When and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I was born in London in 1954, August the 1st.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What academic qualifications do you have?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: High school, after that I got a scholarship to Oxford University and degree in Valencia in Italy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have a limited number of questions related to the Stakic testimony which is now in evidence. At transcript pages 7900 to 7903, you briefly summarised your professional work experience after you finished your studies, so I won't trouble you to repeat it here. I wish to focus first on how you came to visit the camps in Prijedor. You stated at transcript page 7904 that the "Guardian" newspaper which you were working for at the time published an article written by a colleague O'Kane about reports on the Omarska camp. Did Mr. Karadzic respond to the allegations contained in O'Kane's article?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic was in London for a conference sponsored, I think, by the European Union when the allegations were published, and, if you like, invited/challenged us the journalists involved at the "Guardian" and at ITN that he was -- who's guest he was and the programme to come and see for themselves or words to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did he also respond directly to the "Guardian"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He wrote a letter which was published on, I think, the 30th of July saying that there were no camps holding civilians and that the allegations in the "Guardian" were wholly untrue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I can refer you to 65 ter 00413, please. Do you recognise the document that's on the screen?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: That's a printout of the contents of the letter. I should say, perhaps, that I didn't see it on publication. I was on my way to or in Belgrade by then, but I know the text, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender at that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3778, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You state at transcript page 7905 that upon your arrival in Belgrade you spoke with Serb and Bosnian Serb officials and that Nikola Koljevic was the main host. Can you briefly tell the Chamber what was discussed with him?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. We were met by Professor Koljevic who was, as I understand it, Dr. Karadzic's deputy president of the Bosnian Serb Republic, declared republic, and other Serbian officials, and we talked about what we wanted to talk about, our programme, to get to Omarska and Trnopolje as quickly as possible. They wanted to talk about other things, including, and this was of interest, camps in which Serbs were being held prisoner as well on the other side. And we were invited to visit other facilities at which Muslims were being held and I went to one of them. We were -- and I -- we were getting impatient. We thought we were being held up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At transcript page 7908, you gave evidence that you were greeted by Dr. Karadzic upon your arrival in Pale from Belgrade via the federal army helicopter. I'd like to play some footage now. This is 65 ter number 40583A.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: "Penny Marshall: Good morning. Thank you very much indeed for bringing us down. "Karadzic: Thank you for coming here "Penny Marshall: I'm Penny Marshall. "Karadzic: Nice to meet you. We have to make some plan for your journey around Bosnia and Herzegovina. We would like you to see concentration campuses for Serbian civilians held by Muslim forces in the valley of Sarajevo. We'll point for you a few points. Prison then in Tarcin 6 c 20 kilometres from Sarajevo in Silos more than 300 Serbs kept in terrible conditions, all civilians. You will see our [indiscernible], and then you will say what you want to see all around Bosnia-Herzegovina and we'll make a plan for you to be safe. What we are concerned about is that Muslim may try to kill some of you in order to blame us. That's very usual. They do that. Just do some atrocities with foreigners, you know, in order to blame Serbs. They kill their own people in the streets and then they put blame on the Serbs. So we have to make it absolutely secure for you. Then we would like to show you Mr. Panic's way [indiscernible] that will probably be tomorrow about noon, in the afternoon. In Bijeljina, we have arrested 72 independent Serbs who have been disobedient to police or to other. In this area we have been -- we are arrested all of them and they're going to be [indiscernible], and then you could proceed to Bosanska Krajina, Banja Luka, if the corridor is safe. I think it is safe right now. "Penny Marshall: Is that by car or helicopter? "Karadzic: I think by car is much better because they could shoot you by helicopter. So they can reach 150 -- 1.500 metres. They could reach you and kill you. So we have a corridor and I think it's safe still, and we'll get you to Omarska. There you'll join our police and they'll get you to Omarska. You wanted to see Omarska and what else? "Penny Marshall: Trnopolje. "Karadzic: Trnopolje, I will ask ... "Penny Marshall: And Prijedor. "Karadzic: Yeah, that's all in the area. I will ask what's in Trnopolje. In Trnopolje is a kind of a place for stay for people who have no place to stay. This is -- they are not kept by -- by guards. They just have to eat something and they wait to be displaced somewhere, because their villages have been burnt down. They're Serbs and Muslims over there too. "Penny Marshall: Who controls Tarcin? I mean, how can you get us into Tarcin because Tarcin is controlled by Muslims, isn't it? "Karadzic: Yes, that's by Muslims. We can't --"

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Stop the tape there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, I think we just heard you asking Dr. Karadzic that question there.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is the gist of the remainder of the conversation that you had with Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The conversation carried on over lunch and it covered both those issues that we -- we -- it developed both those issues we were talking about. On the film, the camps that we were intend to see and those that Dr. Karadzic wanted to us see on the other side and we had a general conversation over lunch too, which involved discussion of other -- other things so including literature and stuff, but that was the -- those were the parameters of the conversation, more or less. And people came and went.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At transcript page 7910, you state that you left Pale and went by road to Banja Luka via Bijeljina and Brcko and you had a military escort. Was Koljevic part of the convoy?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, I apologise for the sniffling and the coughing. It's just how it is. Yes, Professor Koljevic had been -- joined us in Pale, again having been in Belgrade, and he was, I suppose, our main host along the road. Although not travelling with us in the same vehicle, he popped up for lunch at Bijeljina on the way the place that Dr. Karadzic mentioned in the film where the disobedient Serbs were to be disciplined. We didn't do any more on that, and then he took us as far as Banja Luka where we arrived on the night of the 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At transcript page 7911, you state that the following morning which I think you indicated was the 5th of August, you travelled from Banja Luka to Prijedor escorted by Major Milutinovic and met there a number of persons in the municipal civic centre. If I can just show you a very short piece of video footage. This is Exhibit P3542. And if we can play from 00:22.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: "Omarska, Trnopolje."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, do you recognise the people in this shot?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I did. It's not with me now again. Sorry. Yes. So here we are. We've gone down the chain of command, as it were, Karadzic, Koljevic, Milutinovic, and here we are in Prijedor. And on the left is Milomir Stakic, who was introduced to us as the president of the municipality and Crisis Staff, and next to him second along from the left looking at the screen is Milan Kovacevic, who was introduced to us as Dr. Stakic's deputy of the municipality, the opstina and of the Crisis Committee. We go into keep deep shadow here. I think that's Colonel Arsic there in the middle of the five, introduced to us as the military commander in the region. Next to him, that's the last man along to the right, is Simo Drljaca, introduced to us as the chief of police in Prijedor. All of those four members of the Crisis Staff. And on the end in the pink is Mrs. Balaban whose title we didn't know but she was translating for -- for them at the meeting that was to follow and when we went into the camps -- camp, sorry, in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At transcript pages 7913 to 7935, it deals with the meeting -- with the meeting that you had with the people that you've just identified. You said at the conclusion of the meeting that you went outside and waited there for about 20 minutes or so, and you were then taken to the Omarska camp. Did any other journalists join you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, the meeting went on for quite some time, after which -- during which they wanted us to go to other places, Manjaca, which we didn't want to go to because it had been visited by the Red Cross. And we were then told to go and wait outside, and we did, and talked to some women lining up at the police station worried about the whereabouts of their menfolk, and another journalist from the "Times" and a colleague from "Liberation" of France came along and wanted to join our convoy to my annoyance, professionally speaking, if you appreciate that I didn't want people breezing in on this and they tried to join in, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But were told they couldn't?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, the matter was adjudicated by Simo Drljaca that they couldn't and the reason given was they weren't part of Dr. Karadzic's party. They weren't going at his invitation and on his authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At transcript pages 7939 to 7948, you describe your visit in the camp and mention being present in the canteen when detainees came in for food. Did you interview anyone in the canteen or overhear any interviews being conducted?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, yes. The -- I've testified in the -- in the transcripts that have been submitted about what it was like to see those men and be there, so I won't take your time with that. But, yes, we endeavoured, and perhaps to go back on to something that was said earlier in the introductory remarks, we didn't interview several people. They were too scared to be interviewed. Things were done with -- well, the looks of terror in eyes and things, but, yes, we did interview -- one man only felt -- was emboldened to speak, who I've seen since, and he told us that he -- to summarise it: I do not want to tell any lies but I cannot tell the truth. So the -- as it were, in quotations, the interviews you referred to earlier, there was only one, and really -- and -- but did I speak to another man. I asked what -- how he got a wound on the side of his face. He said he had fallen over. I met him since. He had not fallen over. The wound was otherwise inflicted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could play a short clip from 65 ter number 40168. And this is starting at 12.19 through to 12.54?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: "Penny Marshall [voiceover]: This is all we saw of the prisoners and of Omarska itself. They never spoke. The only voices those of the guards ordering them to eat faster and leave. How are you treated, what are the conditions, I asked? "Unknown person: I don't want to tell lies. I can't speak the truth. Thank you for coming."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And -- and that's your colleague Penny Marshall there in the pink shirt?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, that's Penny Marshall in the pink asking the questions. Actually, I was in shot just on the left sitting at the end of that table, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I now wish to focus on the discussion when you and Penny Marshall and the other reporter, Ian Williams, were trying to get to see the hangar buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, the video we just saw, was it marked as 40168B as one of the associate exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, it's -- that will be C. That will be 40168C. It's a new clip, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So are you tendering that, C?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3779, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: From transcript page 7948 to 7953, a video-tape is played. In the transcript, it has speaker, speaker, speaker, and what's being said, but it's not clear who's doing the -- the talking. And, in fact, at transcript page 7952, what is written in the trial transcript is not a full conversation which is actually contained in the English translation which is -- which is attached to 65 ter number 40437, Your Honours. If he would could play a short video-clip. And this is 65 ter number 40437, starting at 00:44.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you could just pause there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you identify the two people who are in that shot, and that's at :49.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. We're trying to get into the hangar at this point, having seen the canteen earlier. This is Colonel Milutinovic on the left and on the right Simo Drljaca, the chief of police, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could keep playing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: "They could prove --"

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If could you stop there. If you could identify the three people.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The man at the moment talking, gesticulating is called Misa. He was from Belgrade, ITN's interpreter and driver. That's Penny Marshall nearest us. And hidden from view at the moment but there is Ian Williams, who is a reporter also from ITN.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that's at :52. Mr. Zeljko Meakic, he's not in this footage but -- but are you able to distinguish him from the others from what he may have been wearing?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, he was there throughout as well as these other two. He was wearing a beret and I -- comes in and out of the footage at various points. He's come in and out of the day at various points. He had been introduced to us as the commander of Omarska itself, if you like, the end of the line down this chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could keep playing the footage, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: "Guilty or not guilty --"

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Actually, if you could stop. If we go to 2:53, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: "I'm sorry. "You must get some orders. Your wishes are --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could stop there. If we could rewind that tape because this -- and if I could ask the interpreters, please, to interpret what Mrs. Balaban says to Simo Drljaca and what Drljaca responds, please. And if we could take it back to 3:01.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the time-code in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's at the top of page 4, and it starts "Red Cross representative" which is how Mrs. Balaban is described in the actual transcript. And then "guard 2" is how Simo Drljaca has been identified in the -- in the transcript at the top of page 4 of the English. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you could go back to 3:01, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] "Red Cross representative: I explained that our protocol allows us to show only certain things and we cannot contravene this, that is, we need to follow orders. "Guard 2: We cannot. Yes. There are -- and they have all the necessary medical care here, so ... yes they can. "Red Cross representative: You must know we have some orders. Your wishes are ... yes, and your reason is one and our is the other."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we can now continue playing the tape.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: "Penny Marshal: Show us where they live. "Red Cross woman: Oh, well. "Male reporter: Why are you not fulfilling Dr. Karadzic's promise to us? "Red Cross representative: He promised us something else and said you can do this and this and that and not that. If they say this is a protocol of your stay here that will be all. I'm sorry, that will be all. "Male reporter: So he told you, so he told you not to give us access to the majority of this camp? "Red Cross representative: I'm just translating. I'm just trying to do my best. You have now the chance to go to Trnopolje. "Guard: Are we going to Trnopolje?"

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could stop the tape now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, shortly after that you then left for the Trnopolje camp and the video footage of that camp was played at transcript page 7953 to 7959. Was ITN the only TV crew at Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Yes. We were bundled out of Omarska. I mean, the two guards took the safety catches off their guns and things had got very menacing. Sorry. Yes, we went to Trnopolje. No, ITN were not the only crew there. There had been with us since Pale a crew from the Bosnian Serb television. It was unclear for the moment whether they were making their own film about the camps or making a film about us then -- ITN making a film about the camps, and there was also another camera which appeared being operated by a man in military fatigues, and actually the Bosnian Serb TV had military fatigues as well but there was a fourth camera as well which I now know to be that of an intelligence operative of some kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, I'm sorry, I just want to go back to the footage that's on the screen stopping at 4:03. If I can just play it through to 4:11. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: "Red Cross representative: Yes, some security reasons are present here. If you --"

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could just stop it there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you see Mr. Meakic in that shot?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, that's Zeljko Meakic on the left in the beret.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to show you another short video and this is from Exhibit P03697. And if we could play that exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] We would like to live here. We would not like to leave our homes. Could you convey that message? The government -- "Q. Government? There are many governments now."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recognise yourself in that footage?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm at the end there taking notes through the fence. Yes, that's me, and that, I think -- sorry, do you want me to identify other people or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I think the man talking on the microphone at the beginning is the reporter, I think, from the Bosnian Serb television, and that's Penny Marshall there in the pink again, and that's the two of us taking notes through the fence, interviewing the prisoners in the compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to show you another short video and this is from 65 ter 40168 and this will be part D. If the footage can run from 14:11?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we please have a page reference. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: There won't be any need for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: "They promised to show us the second camp Trnopolje where 2.000 refugees are living. We were not prepared for what we saw and heard there."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could stop that there and that's at 14:26.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recognise anyone in this shot?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I recognise Fikret Alic shaking Penny Marshall's hand through the wire and others I know by sight but not by name.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But did you interview Fikret Alic that day?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: He told us that this group -- he told me that this group had arrived, this group in the compound that we can see had arrived at Trnopolje that morning from another camp, the name of which was new to me, Keraterm, and he and others talked about a terrible night in Keraterm when something like between 130 and 150 people were killed in one night. This young man Fikret Alic said that he had been tasked to be part of the dispatch loading the bodies up onto the -- with bulldozers onto trucks but that he had broken down and not been able to -- in his place taken by an older prisoner. And there was a conversation with some of the other men about their arrival from these -- mostly from Keraterm, but I understood some had come from Omarska as well that very day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we then play from 17:25 to 17:32, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: "No one we spoke to knew why they had been brought here, whether they were prisoners, refugees, or what lay in store for them."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, you see the barbed wire and other types of wire. Was this how it was?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, they were in a compound, and it was a guarded compound, as we can see, and they'd come from these other camps that morning. And it was for us, really, to try and ascertain why, which I, in part, did that day. It was very chaotic in Trnopolje and was able to establish definitely later, a few days later, when, as you said in your summary, we went over the mountains in the convoy of deportees because these people were here for enforced deportation, and we accompanied them to illustrate that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You stated at transcript page 7959 that you went into the medical centre and met with Dr. Idriz Merdzanic. Who else was with you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: In the -- well, it's called the medical centre. They had to scavenge for their medicines. None were provided, although the Red Cross was there. In the medical centre was Idriz Merdzanic, and another assistant of his -- or a colleague, I should say, of his, Azra Blazevic, who was a vet, using her medical abilities as best she could help. And, well, the ITN crew was there. I was by the door while Dr. Merdzanic was interviewed. And patients coming in and out. Other orderlies in there too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could show a short clip. 65 ter number 40168 and start it at 6:53 and stop at 7:40, 7:44.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: "... the camp. The pictures show severe injuries, apparently as a result of beatings. In the makeshift medical centre, there were cases of scabies, malnutrition and diarrhoea. Local doctors said they were chronically short of medicines and drugs. Among them was a Muslim doctor. We asked him whether there had been any cases of beatings. "Yes. "Many?"

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you were there while that was being filmed?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just standing in the doorway.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender those portions of -- and I think Mr. Reid has ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Both of them are under D?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No. Mr. Reid would rather they were individual -- be given individual alphabetical numbers at the end of each of the separate clips. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the footage of Mr. Fikret Alic was 40168D will be admitted as Exhibit P3780, is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the footage of makeshift -- so-called makeshift medical centre will be --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, there's one in between that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The barbed wire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That will be admitted as Exhibit P3781.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the last one admitted as Exhibit 3782.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So, Mr. Vulliamy, from Trnopolje did you return immediately to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. We decided to return because I think -- I think the plan had been for us to remain in Banja Luka, but the ITN translator/driver, Misa, whom I pointed out, inferred that we were not safe. Things had gotten quite acrimonious between us and our hosts by then and we elected to get back to Belgrade as soon as possible and, well, to communicate with our offices, really, because we needed to know what to do with the material we had and so we went back to Belgrade that night. This was the time before any kind of mobile communications [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And at transcript page 7977 to 7979, you mention having English tea with Professor Koljevic and that he made a rather barbed joke at the expense of the media in the world?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, it was a valid one too. Professor Koljevic was a professor of English and an Anglophile and he invited me to tea at the Hyatt Hotel, and his joke was, sort of, that it took us -- it took us so long to find these camps. He joked that they were so near Venice, and he had a joke at my and our collective expense that all we cared about was the siege of sophisticated Sarajevo and how long it had taken us to find these camps and I -- I thought, in a rather dark way, he had a point, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to show you another short video. This is the final video I will show you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's 65 ter number 40154 and this is from point 57:29.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: "Anchorman: Dr. Karadzic, the Serb president of Yugoslavia, Mr. Panic has said that he's ordering you to shut camps like Omarska and Trnopolje within 30 days. Can you do that? "Karadzic: I can do that even within two days if Muslim side accept our proposal of exchange of war prisoners on the type 'all to all.' We have offered many times to Muslim side that kind of thing and they didn't accept. "Anchorman: So what you're saying is it's most unlikely that his will happen? "Karadzic: No. If they don't accept, we will quit those prisoners, prisons; these are really not camps, these are prisons, but anyway we'll treat them, we'll release all of those people, no matter they are war prisoners, no matter they are going to attack us again "Anchorman: Now, you know the outcry that there has been following ITN's reports. We couldn't see all of the camp in Omarska. You say the people there in the camps running them are undisciplined. Therefore, would you agree now to go back to that particular camp with our reporter Penny Marshall so that we can see everything there with you guiding us round? "Karadzic: Yes, absolutely. Would I like to join you there, because I would see what people are disobedient and who is responsible for so much -- so few food that people get. I know that all people don't have enough food but still prisoners would have at least two meals a day. "Anchorman: So that is a promise from you. You are ready to go with our reporter straight away to that -- "Karadzic: Absolutely, that's my duty. That's our duty to make people suffer as less as we can do. "Anchorman: And so the challenge is taken up. You will go with us - what - within the next 24 hours? "Karadzic: Twenty-four hours. It may happen also within 24 hours. "Anchorman: Well, we would like to hear you say very clearly, Dr. Karadzic, that you will go within 24 hours. "Karadzic: You can go within 24 hours, and I hope I could -- I could make it for myself within 24 hours because we have big Muslim offensive in city of Sarajevo. Very, very heavy fights today going on. "Anchorman: Very well. The suspicion must be that where our cameras are not allowed to go, and perhaps in other places, that terrible things are happening. There's talk of allegations that have been made of beatings, executions or whatever. Are you sure, yourself, that these things are not happening in camps run by Serbs, Bosnian Serbs? "Karadzic: We have 13 prisons and the prison of Omarska is the worst one. And we wanted these journalists to see the worst one not to see the best one in order to help people and in order to show all the faces of this terrible civil war which was caused by premature recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina for what is very responsible European Community. We are ready to open any corner of this country, any prison of this country to Red Cross. It was invited by me this morning and to any journalist and to any international commission. "Anchorman: Dr. Karadzic in Belgrade, thank you very much indeed"

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you and that stops at 1:00:46.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, you've reviewed this footage since you've been in The Hague. Have you seen it before?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, I hadn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Are you able to place a date on with when it was broadcast?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It's obviously an immediate reaction to -- to the outcry that followed ITN's initial report. I was, by then, on my way to the other side to see where the Serbian prisoners was -- were being held as charged by Dr. Karadzic. So it would be either August the 7th or the 8th that would be corroborated.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic made a number of comments. He said that Omarska was the worst camp. Is this how he described it to you when you had met him in Pale a few days earlier?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, it wasn't at all how he described Omarska and -- but as it turned out following my subsequent inquiries, he was right, I think. It was terrible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And when you say subsequent to your inquiries, what are you referring to then?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Besides the visit I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know how much of this is in interest to the Court, but I've been working on this on and off or the past two decades. That was 19 years ago, and I have met many of the former inmates since Omarska and Trnopolje. I've think I've interviewed -- I should -- well, if not hundreds scores of them, and, yes, I think Dr. Karadzic's assessment is probably right that of the camps that were being - where he calls them prisons, I call them camps -- being held by the Bosnian Serbs, Omarska was -- was the worst, it seems, from the things that were happening in there that I've been able to decipher and hear from the survivors, otherwise -- but that's hearsay. I'm at your disposal on that. And -- and certainly his remarks in that film did seem to confirm the impression given when we met him in Pale, as you're asking me, that he had authority. I mean, he says: Well never mind 30 days, I can close them within two. And that was certainly the impression we had in Pale that we were going there on his authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you're aware of journalists who visited the camp again?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I can't testify to that. I know that a great media circus descended on the camps, especially Trnopolje, because I've seen lots of footage on that on August the 7th, 8th, 9th-ish I wouldn't know, because however it may sound now, I took Dr. Karadzic's remarks seriously when we were talking in Pale, and by the -- on the day of August the 8th, I think it was, early in the morning or late on the 7th, I was heading round to the -- you can't cross lines. I was driving through Hungary to go over to the other side to make inspections and to endeavour to get into camps where Serbian prisoners were being held which I did, so I wasn't actually there when the media circus descended on -- on Trnopolje and Omarska, but certainly there were a large number of them went back, I mean, the sort of -- by which time, as I understand from the films, the places had been changed quite a bit, and I've certainly done a lot of interviews with survivors of Omarska about how that place was part emptied out and part cleaned up in readiness for these visits, as was Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If -- and then finally, you interviewed Dr. Kovacevic in 1996 along with Dr. Stakic, and this is in your Stakic transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, I'm minded to tender that video-clip.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3783, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And, Ms. Sutherland, I remember that you showed us the original video-clip that -- in which Mr. Karadzic gave some general introduction to the journalist.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which was 40583A --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- which hasn't been admitted, will now be.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P3784, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then Mr. Reid advises me that there were two other clips played from 65 ter number 40437.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. 40437, yes. That will be admitted as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 3785, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Vulliamy, can you recognise this document that's coming up on the screen, please?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, that's a typewritten transcript of the conversation with Dr. Kovacevic in 1996. I went back with a colleague from "The New York Times" to see him and Dr. Stakic and Dr. -- and Professor Koljevic and we endeavoured to see Simo Drljaca, who refused to see us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that's dealt with in your Stakic transcript?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes that's --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: -- exhibited that we've [indiscernible]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender these notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3786, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And thank you, Mr. Vulliamy. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we deal with the remaining associate exhibits, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are tendering 65 ter number 19683 and 19684. I think there are some confusion in uploading the -- in e-court. Should we upload 19683 first. It's 65 ter number 19683. It says it's allegedly a copy of relevant parts of the book "Seasons in Hell."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, pages 8 and 9 and pages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But we'll see. What I think what is uploaded is different. I think this is a duplicate of --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- 65 ter number 19685.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, you're correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we upload 19684 then? This is the copy of "Seasons in Hell."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and that is at 19683 and it's also at 19708. 19708 is excerpts of chapter 5 of the book written by Mr. Vulliamy, and the excerpts that were tendered in Stakic were pages 98 to 107. And, in fact, at 19683, that includes pages 100 to 101 so they're actually included in 19708. So we would simply need to tender pages 8 and 9 and then pages 98 to 107, and I will ensure that those are uploaded into e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In one number or in two separate numbers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just wondering in order to make sense of the Stakic transcript ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Into --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- two separate numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We were to keep them separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And there are in relation to notes taken by the witnesses during the interviews of Dr. Kovacevic and Dr. Stakic, you already tendered 19691, but both of them have several 65 ter numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's -- what has a lot of 65 ter numbers, and this is on page 4 of the 92 ter notification filed on the 2nd of November, are the actual shorthand notes that Mr. Vulliamy read into the record and Judge Schomburg required that they were read page by page by page, and so unfortunately then they were given this one, one, two, three, four, five -- eight different 65 ter number in our case. In fact, they could be given one for each of those shorthand notes, for Dr. Kovacevic interview and Dr. Stakic interview, and then of course, we have the -- also the typewritten version which the Stakic typewritten notes were an associated exhibited, and I just tendered this morning the typewritten notes of Kovacevic meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit them in one document per -- for -- per interviewees.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One further questions you tendered 40168C until F, but I'm not sure the 40618B has been uploaded into e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, can you repeat that number again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it's not in the e-court. Could you release it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Reid will release it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I'm not sure whether it's 65 ter number 40438 has been also uploaded in the e-court. So while you will see to it, that, I'm asking Mr. Robinson whether Defence has any objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then subject to those -- or the supplementation, those will be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And will be given numbers in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Vulliamy your evidence in lieu of examination-in-chief has been admitted in written form and now you will be further asked by Mr. Karadzic in his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Karadzic. Dobro jutro.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dobro jutro. Thank you. Good morning. I would like to us to take advantage of the fact that you wrote this book, so let us briefly go through the book. Let us look at some parts of your book.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we please have this in e-court. 04807, 1D04807, 1D.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, page 4. So this is the cover of your book, isn't it? I wanted to ask you about this dedication. This book of yours, is it dedicated to the victims of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and can you tell us which one of these is a Serb?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Am I reading off -- is this an accurate translation on my screen? I'm hearing nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you check.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Doesn't matter because I can read it. The answer is none, sir. I can hear anything, but I can read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, you should hear that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can hear myself, but I couldn't hear Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you repeat your question, just in case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, this was my question: Since you dedicated this book to the victims in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I was interested in hearing which one of these was a Serb?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: These are individual dedicatees. None of them is Serbian. I wasn't able to work on the Serbian side during the first year of the war covered by this book because I wasn't given permission after we went over on the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have a look at page 7 in e-court. The next one. The next one. I would like to draw your attention to the shadowed part. What you say there is that you will be accused of being pro-Muslim, whatever that means. Could you please take a look at that.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you really think that's the way it was? Do you really think that you managed to maintain your objectivity? Do you really think that these accusations are unfounded?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I'm grateful to you for raising this. The word I should have used there is neutral, that we remain neutral over the most appalling racialist violence. I have been ask by this before, and I think it's in the transcripts that Your Honours have. Objectivity -- and I can see it a mistaken word here. I should have said we remain neutral. Where something is fact specific, I remain objective. I mean, if you go into a house and you see six bodies, it's not 12 because they're Muslim or 3 because they're Serbs or whatever it's -- it's six. What I am saying here, and I stand by it, is that I make -- I do not attempt to try and be neutral. I'm not neutral between the camp guards and the prisoners, between the raped women and the rapists, and I don't -- I can't in all honesty sit here in court and say that I am or want to be or -- or -- can be neutral over this kind of violence and when I had -- this book is about the first year of the war, and it takes us from the -- the camps, the discovery of the camps, the corralling and enforced deportation over the mountains, and the second part is to do with, if you like, a different part of the war involving the Bosnian Croats, and I do not claim to be neutral over the sort of violence I was witnessing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm interested in this particular wording, racialist violence. Do you think that we had quarreled there on the basis of racial differences? Do you know that Serbs believe that Muslims are also Serbs who converted to Islam and that is what Lord Owen thinks as well?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I heard the Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina or Bosniaks, or whatever we were going to call them, often referred to as Balija, which equates as, sort of, filthy Gypsy, but the -- who converted to who to what religion or what Lord Owen things is really of -- well, it's for Your Honours to ask Lord Owen, I suppose, but what I -- the reason I used the word "racialist" was because it seemed to me pretty clear, very clear, that the -- in the camps the inmates were either Bosnian Muslims or Croats and that the guards and the people running them were Bosnian Serbs, and in the latter part of the book which perhaps doesn't concern you so much but did me, it was very much the heraldry and insignia of Croatia or of Herzegovina, I should say, perhaps that was being used in this violence. Certainly the iconography in the name which this appalling violence was taking place was very much Serbian, and I do concede that there was violence on the other side as well in the name of the Muslim side, but I think that if you -- where I come from, if one self-defined ethnicity seeks to obliterate or to clear the territory of all members of another ethnicity and to obliterate any memory of them, that is racialism.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll get to that. I wanted to ask you whether you know that George Kenney does not belong to this group. He is a harsh critic of his own government and the West because of their partiality, vis-a-vis the Muslim who is abused that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I met George Kenney during the writing of this book and I'm aware that he changed -- he changed his position on things. I haven't spoken to him since.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the next page now. Page 12, could we have that in e-court. Seven in e-court. I apologise. On the right-hand side, could you please take a look at where it says "Bosnia-Herzegovina" and then "Greater Serbia." So you proceeded from the celebration of the 600th anniversary of the battle of Kosovo. Do you really think that that's the way it was, that there were only -- that there were almost 2 million drunkards there and that this was a problematic speech made by President Milosevic. The Western politicians at the time considered him to be moderate. You refer to that event as the beginning of all of these developments.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I think most of the coverage -- I wasn't there. Most of the coverage sees that speech as being an important rallying cry. As regards the alcohol there seems to be little doubt about that, unless I'm to be corrected. And I think that was in -- in all the written accounts I've read of the -- the rise of President Milosevic, that was seen as a -- as a -- as a moment whereby he connected very much to -- to the people and began this change of the language of Marxism of which his party had hitherto been an adherent to a more nationalistic and more aggressively nationalistic politics, and that he -- I won't say used, but that this was -- this particular speech at this moment was in all the writing I've -- I've read. And, by all means, call the historians themselves that there was a converge on the opinion that this was an important moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, did you notice that at the time, not historians later, but at the time Western analysts and politicians consider this to be a moderate speech? Also, statesmen from all the Yugoslav Republics were present there. They sat in the first row.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I have no doubt they were all there. Yugoslavia was still Yugoslavia then, and no doubt many Western -- people in the West did think Milosevic was moderate. Some of them still do. What ensued and from this speech and his Presidency I -- I -- I don't regard as moderate. For what it's worth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So do we agree that this bit about drunkards, alcohol in general, that that's a bit of an exaggeration?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I haven't read a -- as it were, a sort of a -- a piece of reportage about the rally that then include reference to people having a few drinks. I'm not saying it's such a bad thing. It's just what apparently happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have pages 66 and 67 in the book, but it's page 8 in e-court. The previous one, actually, please. Yes, that's it. Could you please take a look at the right-hand side where you speak about Mr. Izetbegovic. This is what you say and I'm going to read it out in English: [In English] [As read] "Izetbegovic was determined to keep Bosnia-Herzegovina as a unitary multi-ethnically republic. The secretary sectarian exclusively Muslim SDA was hardly the way to achieve it. And Izetbegovic put a second blot on his -- his [indiscernible] soon after becoming president of the republic. In March 1991, the Portuguese presidency hosted a meeting of EC leaders in Lisbon to discuss dividing Bosnia-Herzegovina into regions in which the three ethnic groups would enjoy spheres of influence. It was partitioned with a sugar coating and enthusiastically agreed to by Tudjman and Milosevic. Izetbegovic, with a shortsightedness that has baffled his people ever since, opened the door to the thin end of ...," [Interpretation] could we have the next page, [In English] "... the wedge and backed the idea. Two days later he was forced to eat crow, apparently realising his blunder and with characteristic naivety withdrawing his acceptance of the EC's Greek rift. Despite his Muslim nationalism, Izetbegovic was -- has argued from the outset that Bosnia cannot be ethnically partitioned because it is impossible without ethnic cleansing. Our ethnic map is intermingled like a Jackson Pollock painting. There are no ethnically pure regions." [Interpretation] So you were fully aware of what the solution was. However you thought that Izetbegovic made a mistake because he accepted the reorganisation of Bosnia. Do you agree that that was not a partition or division but this was decentralisation according to regions?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Sorry. I didn't quite understand your question. Did the Lisbon discourse -- was decentralisation but not partition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that according to the Lisbon agreement Bosnia would remain a single country with external borders and inside there would be three regions that would be rather autonomous?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I think that was the idea of -- of what they were trying to do at Lisbon was to -- was to have a -- rather than the two entities or statelets that we now have, they were going to try to divide Bosnia in -- in -- into some kind of ethnic canton system, and in that passage I'm trying to really, I suppose, deal with -- with then President Izetbegovic's meandering around this. I don't know how much the Court wants to listen to a discussion about Izetbegovic, but he -- he changed his mind quite a lot on whether he wanted cantons, partition, a unitary state. But to that Lisbon agreement I referred to was, yes, sir, it was -- was to do with a cantonisation along ethnic grounds. We agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know why Mr. Izetbegovic gave up on this agreement that had already been accepted?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I -- I -- I can't -- I don't -- I sort of -- I don't try to mind-read President Izetbegovic either in retrospect or at the time, but I certainly noted that he -- that he was ready to accept things that he then went on to reject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I meant that you had heard or read about him being persuaded by a diplomat to reject this and ask for more. However you haven't heard about that. We're going to abandon that particular topic. When you testified in other cases, did you observe that after the secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the difference between the Serbs and the Croats was considerably smaller than the difference between the Serbs and the Muslims or the Croats and the Muslims respectively, in terms of their political views concerning the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm just going to examine your question carefully, sir. The differences between the Serbs and the Croats -- yes. I understood and understand that discussions were had as regarding the partition of Bosnia between Serbian -- a Serbian sphere of influence and a Croatian sphere of influence with a Muslim bit, if you like, and that conversations were had between, as I understand it, President Milosevic and President Tudjman of Croatia with regard to that. So I suppose you could say that the influence -- the difference between the Serbs and the Croats was smaller inasmuch as neither of them wanted to be part of a country or necessarily part of a country called Bosnia-Herzegovina as long as it was dominated by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, I did not mean Presidents Milosevic and Tudjman. I meant myself and Boban, or rather, Boban and myself. You noted that there were lesser differences there. Not in terms of the details where things would be, but in terms of what Bosnia would be like as a whole in the future. The Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Serbs, if I can call them that conditionally, were in favour of a decentralised Bosnia consisting of three entities, whereas the Muslim side wanted to have a unitary Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I -- the term "Muslim side," I think one could say that a very considerable number of people who are called Muslims and many people of -- many Croats and many Serbs saw themselves as wanting to be -- to live in Bosnia. Political movements representing considerable numbers of Serbs, yours and Croats, Mr. Boban's, wanted not to live in a -- in a united country and wanted to demonstrate their demands and to show their affiliations to respectively Belgrade and Zagreb. What concerns me in the book, really, because this isn't a political book, is what was then done by, shall we say, the nationalist interests of the Bosnian Serbs and the nationalist interests of the Bosnian Croats to establish and carve out the territories that they did not want to be governed from Sarajevo. I mean, there's a jump between the policy to mass murder, and it's up -- it's up to the Court how much we want to go into the politics, but I do concede that you led a movement that did not want to be governed from Sarajevo and that Mr. Boban led a movement that did not want to be governed from Sarajevo. Obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now let me ask you this: Do you agree that Bosnia and Herzegovina had a Christian majority, taking into account both us Serbs and Bosnian Croats together and that Christian majority was in favour of a decentralised tripartite Bosnia, whereas the Muslim minority was in favour of a unitary Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm struggling to understand the relevance of these lines of questions. We are due to take a break soon. After the break, I would like you to concentrate on his -- his evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I accept your suggestions, as usual, but this witness had written a book, and from it I saw what his understanding of our crisis was. That is his vantage point, and that is very important for the second part of my examination when I'm going to shed light on things that the Defence does not agree about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And that's why we allowed you to proceed. We'll take a break for half an hour now and resume at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's finish with the book, according to the Trial Chamber's guidance. Let's look at page 11 in e-court, please. Can the left-hand side be displayed. You're talking about the embargo, about the difficulties experienced by the Muslim side with regard to the purchasing of weapons, and then at the bottom of the page you say that you were aware of a perverse smuggling route along which guns paid for by the Muslims using money from Turkey and the Arab countries would arrive at the Croatian port of Rijeka. And then can we look at the top of the right-hand side page. And then you describe how the Croats would take a half cut; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: As I understood it from a number of sources, Bosnian government military, HVO Croatian military, and international intelligence, this was the deal that pertained to some of the arms shipments. I can't speak for all of them. That as the front and central Bosnian, at least, became progressively cut off, they would get a quarter of the weapons that would arrive in Rijeka, or indeed later by plane, and that there would be a sort of commission, if you like, of 50 per cent to the HV and another 25 per cent for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go back to the left half of the same page. You say here that the parliament at Pale rejected Vance-Owen's plan. UN Secretary of State Warren Christopher replied that the lifting of the embargo [In English] Simply leveled the killing field. [Interpretation] Do you remember that I, myself, accepted the Vance-Owen Plan but that the parliament actually rejected it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that, sir. And I remember you accepting a number of plans, and -- as well and there were innumerable treaties, all of which ended up in nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You, therefore, know that I accepted the Carrington-Cutileiro Plan, the Vance-Owen Plan, the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, that I did not accept the Contact Group plan, but I accepted the Dayton Accord. There was just one plan that I did not accept; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I -- from memory, I -- I can't remember which plans you did or didn't accept, but I do remember you accepting the Vance-Owen Plan, and of course the Dayton agreement. I mean, if you'll pardon the sort of implied exhaustion and cynicism of this on the ground the Vance-Owen Plan came and went and it didn't really amount to much. I mean, there were negotiations going on two days before the Srebrenica massacre, I mean -- but, yes, you accept the Vance-Owen Plan, and I'll leave it to the experts to -- to regard to the others. From memory, here and now, I can't actually remember which ones you didn't accepted, but you did -- there were endless plans, treaties, none of which amounted to very much on the ground. The killing carried on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To finish with the book, I would like to ask you this: I'm a little bit confused by the part of your CV and the bibliography where you refer to only two books, "Agriculture of Bosnia-Herzegovina" by Mustafa Imamovic and "Bosnia and Bosniaks" by Rusmir Mahmutcehajic. These are the only two books that you refer to in the bibliography of your book. Those are local sources. Rusmir Mahmutcehajic was a politician at the time. Was that enough for you to understand the Bosnian knot?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The Bosnia knot. I'm looking at "History of the Yugoslav Peoples" by Fred Singleton here. There were, of course, books about Yugoslavia and Tito and the South Slav region going right through the ages which I have read. I think mine and a book by Misha Glenny were the only ones on the wall that had appeared, along the post 1992 period, that had -- that had been written up until this point. This book was written, Your Honours, when, for the most part, during the summer of 1993 with everything in full flow and published a few months later. There weren't many, if any, books about what was going on around me at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's skip the part that refers to Croatia. You were in Croatia, and you saw for yourself there what was the nature and the cruelty of the civil war that was raging there, and then in the Stakic case, on the 14th of July, on pages 735, 736, you testified that you had seen the fear of Serbs in Croatia, that you had spoken to them about that and that you had experienced and seen what they had experienced in the country, in the making that was Croatia at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I'd covered that -- that war in 1991, and I had covered both the Croatians' aspirations to fight a war of independence and the -- the fears of the Serbian populations in being part of that Croatia, the independent Croatia. There was an element of -- and I think I've put it similarly in -- in the past. A element of at least agreement over what was being fought over albeit from completely different sides in that war. There were -- there was an aspiration for independence by the Croats and a willingness to fight for it, and there were fears among the Serbs and a willingness to -- to fight that independence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I reported suffering on both sides and violence by both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt, but just on page 41, line 17, there's reference to "then you testified in the Stakic case, on the 14th of July, on pages 735 and 736." Unfortunately, the Kovacevic case and the Stakic case have the same case number, and so if we're talking about July, we're talking about 1998 in the Kovacevic case, and in -- the Stakic case was in September 2002. So it was simply to make the record clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, and I would like to thank you on behalf of the Defence. We will try to deal with that as best as we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the Prlic et al. case, which is 1D04800 on the transcript page 1726, you confirmed that you were more than aware that the JNA had attacked Croatia. Wouldn't you say that was all one country and that the JNA was duty-bound by the constitution to preserve the territorial integrity of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Croatian independence -- forgive me if I don't have the dates in my head exactly. It's -- it's, I think, difficult to talk about exactly when Yugoslavia can be said to have ceased to exist and exactly when Croatia came to exist. Certainly the perceptions were different from Belgrade and from Zagreb. Certainly the Yugoslav Army with Yugoslavia insignia on the tanks outside and Serbian insignia on the walls inside the barracks was attacking and -- the Croatian town of Vukovar fairly ferociously, and similarly the embryonic Croatian Army which called itself various things at various points was attacking the JNA, and at what point it -- it became Croatia and ceased to be Yugoslavia is a matter for -- for examination beyond my -- my recollections of the exact dates of declarations and -- and conflict in my head now, but I -- at some point along the line Croatia declares independence and it becomes a war between Serbia and Croatia. But at the beginning, yes, indeed, it was the JNA, Yugoslav National Army in combat with Croatian secessionists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender that book pages that we have displayed into evidence. They are number 1D04807. The Defence may be of assistance to the Registry with regard to the page numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we add it to the Prosecution exhibit or admit it separately?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any observations, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Well, only to say that Mr. Karadzic was citing certain pages in e-court, page 7 or page 12 or whatever, and it may be easier when you're reviewing the record to have it as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's follow that submission. We'll admit it as Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D1897, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to move on to London. During the London Conference, I contested some allegations about camps and then I invited British journalists, whoever wanted to go there, to come and that entire Republika Srpska will be open to them to see whatever they wanted to see. Do you remember? I was not provoked into doing that. I was the one who invited British journalists to come and see for themselves what was going on.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, I agree. I don't see -- I don't see that you were -- provoked isn't the word I would use. Challenged perhaps by the allegations that had been published in the "Guardian" and in an American paper called "Newsday," and your response was, and I summarise, not your words, but the sense of it were, "Well, come and see for yourselves on my authority." And you contested that the -- the allegations of brutality in the camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I would like to call up 1D4821 in e-court. I believe that you will be able to help us and tell us whether this is your first report about your visit to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: That's it, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was before the media circus, as you call it, that fell upon Bosnia. At this particular point in time, there was still no media circus; right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's right. Perhaps Your Honours might like to note it says the "Toronto Star" at the top. It's a reprint. I believe the date is the same, I don't know. Sorry. Yes, that's before the media circus.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at the first paragraph in the report. For example, the framed part. Here you state with full responsibility that you had been informed that the Omarska camp was an investigation centre operated by the Bosnian-Serbian police for Muslim captives near Prijedor in Northern Bosnia; right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to read everything else. Everybody can do it for themselves. You say that there was a meal in five minutes. "They first wanted to eat and then talk to me." Can we go to the following page. Again, the first frame where you say that Omarska was a mine and that the Bosnian government referred to it as one of the 57 concentration camps. And then you say that the unexpected access was as part of an invitation by the Bosnian Serb president, Radovan Karadzic, to inspect whatever we wanted to see. One of your interlocutors said that he was a member of the Defence forces but he was not captured in combat. He tried to get to Trnopolje, which was a transit civilian camp, but the army caught him on the way. Is that what the person told you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was your impression then that fighting in Prijedor had started on the 22nd of May and that it had lasted for six weeks and that was the length of the war in Bosnia. There was no war in Prijedor, and that between the 21st of May and the 2nd of June there was a lot of fighting going on and that this particular person speaks about those fights; right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: My knowledge of what had happened in the area prior to August the 5th when we arrived was that there had been what I would -- or what was being described as some sort of takeover or even a coup of the town at the end of April. Yes, there had been some sporadic resistance to the -- the new order, if you like, and there had been, variously, demands for villages to hand over weapons. Some had, some hadn't. But from the -- and I must not talk with hindsight because I've been working on this for many, many years.
