We saw on the way to the camp signs of -- of -- of very heavy destruction, particularly around Kozarac, which we skirted along the main road. The vast majority of houses burned out and their -- the inhabitants gone. There had obviously been some exchanges. This man speaking had been a member of some sort of defence. The surrenders had been, as I understand it, pretty quick. They had been overpowered very swiftly with an overwhelming force. That's how I understood it. I did not think there was any sign of fighting in the area at this time, any -- if there had been any resistance, it had been totally subjugated. There was a mock battle on the way to the camp. You, when we met in Pale, sir, did talk about fears for our own safety and -- and attempts to kill us by the Muslims that -- would then be blamed on you in the film we saw. There was a rather sort of ridiculous prank whereby our convoy was "attacked," but actually it turned out to be by our own hosts by way of a sort of prank, but there was no fighting when we visited. I had some experience of warfare by then and could tell that these shots were going over our heads and the return fire was going high into the air. It was a silly thing to try and make us afraid and to put us off. There was no fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us just limit ourselves to what you know exactly, what you learned and saw at the time. Let me mind you just briefly. On page 3 you told us that you had passed through Brcko and that there was a lot of damage in Brcko. Do you know who controlled Brcko at the time? Let me help you. Do you agree that you had passed through the Serbian territory and that the Brcko that you saw was the Serbian part of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: As I understood it, because we were in Serb -- Bosnian Serb vehicles, the part of Brcko we passed through was in the hands of the Bosnian Serbs, and there were large areas of the town shelled, bombed, burnt out, and deserted, which I inferred would be where the Muslims had lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But why didn't you ask who -- who was it who had shelled Brcko, which was in Serbian hands? Do you think that it was the Serbs themselves who shelled Brcko?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: There wasn't -- there wasn't any -- we were in our own vehicle at that point, and Professor Koljevic was in another vehicle. I understood it -- I understood at the time that -- well, there obviously had been fighting in Brcko and whoever had lived in those houses didn't live there any more, and so the town was under the control of the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It is my thesis that all that time you could only be passing through the Serbian territory and that everything that you saw and that was destroyed was destroyed by the opposition side who shelled us. Do you -- do you agree that you passed through the corridor west of Brcko which at place was only a couple of hundred metres wide?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I didn't know exactly how wide it was, but I knew there was a corridor, yes, that connected Bijeljina, Brcko, and Serbia proper to the Banja Luka region, and that we passed through it, and that it was narrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that there was not a single day without fire being opened on the corridor, would you then accept that our fear for you was justified? Not a singe day -- there are reports to that effect. There was not a single day that passed without fire being opened on the corridor?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, I was obviously grateful for your concern for our safety, and we were lucky to get one of the days when there wasn't fighting, thankfully. The first shots we heard was when there was this prank I discussed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm contesting precisely that. Do you know that in Prijedor and around it until late 1994 there were guerrilla Muslim groups that lived in the woods in dugouts and that from time to time they would go out and kill soldiers and villagers? While you were there, there were a lot of them, and there were a certain number of them until the end of 1994.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: To my knowledge at the time, there had been exchanges of fire but that the -- any resistance had been subjugated. Colonel Milutinovic did explain to us when we asked him about all the bombed and burnt out houses that 40.000 Muslims had left the area and implied that they had done so of their own accord. There were still some people living in intact houses, which was slightly bizarre to behold, I have to say, and it was explained that these were the Serbs that had remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us conclude with this page. Here Sabahudin told you about the investigating measures, that there were -- that were applied and that he told you the truth; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. He'd been investigated and -- and he hadn't been beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we go to the bottom of the page, please. Here you report that Omarska is an investigation centre for men suspected of taking part in the Muslim irregular army. You say that they were rounded up there to be screened in order to determine whether they were fighters or civilians. We can see here that you observed the 80 inmates and that you saw no signs of beatings. I asked you the same thing during -- when we discussed the interview. Could you have -- sorry. Let's go to something else. A moment ago, you said they were attacked by Serb forces. If I told you that Prijedor was attacked by Muslim forces, what would you say? If I told you that it wasn't the Serbs who attacked Prijedor but that they were, rather, defending the town -- the town centre and managed to do so.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I saw very little sign of shelling in the centre of Prijedor. None, in fact, that I can recall. Or put it this way: To contrast the damage of Kozarac with the centre of Prijedor, we're talking about two completely different landscapes. The centre of Prijedor, I recall, as being more or less intact as I think the films show, and I certainly recall them being intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we go to the next page, please. In the meantime, I wish to ask you the following: Did you know that the Green Berets on the 30th of May managed to reach the very town centre? They launched a surprise attack reaching the town centre and that they were only defeated after two or three days.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that the Green Berets had fought this battle, nor did I see any signs of the battle in the centre of the town or any of the parts that we visited in Prijedor. There was a little damage around but very -- I mean, compared to the surroundings, nothing really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm afraid that on page 15, line 21; we have something missing in the transcript. Ms. Balaban then said, "I am only interpreting," when she explained her position to the journalists. Could this be verified by Registry or whoever's in charge of LiveNote. Let's look at this, please. Here you say that you could observe that Omarska and Trnopolje were run by civilian authorities and that you were told that no one was proud of it. In the boxed part, it says: [In English] "Though this may be true of Omarska, it is generally untrue since a camp we visited on the outskirts of Sarajevo has been established solely for the purpose of swapping Muslim captives for Serbs." [Interpretation] Which prison did you see exactly which served that purpose?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: This is the Kula prisons on -- on the outskirts as I said of Sarajevo which we visited on the same day that, Your Honours, we met with Dr. Karadzic. And it -- well, I think I've described it and describe it as a sad place. There's nothing particularly to -- to complain about, to write about. If I could, sorry, just make something to the record of my own. Apologise. Dr. Karadzic has said that I described Omarska as an investigation centre. The record doesn't show that that is in inverted commas. That is very much their term during interminable briefings we were given upstairs. I'm not calling it an investigation centre, I'm putting that in quotation marks, that's what they called it. And the record, as written -- Dr. Karadzic quotes from the article correctly, but it's in inverted commas which indicates that that is what they were calling it. I'm sorry, just to make sure it's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know, were you told that Kula had been a prison for a while for misdemeanor detainees and it remained being a prison throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: We were told that it was a prison we were told that the people in there at the time of our visit were there awaiting exchange, and that is actually, I think, what most of those men said themselves, that they hoped to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you see anyone at Kula who was not fit for military service?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I would think that -- and this is my recollection at a distance. I put that in the article to give some sense of balance and to put Omarska in context of -- I didn't want to write much more about Kula. I would think, thinking back, that some of them were probably a little old to fight very effectively. Others were of fighting age, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that Mr. Izetbegovic, as of the 4th of April and up until your visit, on a number of occasions ordered a general mobilisation of all those who were fit for military service, and did you know that there was basically a hundred per cent response by Muslims to that call?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I didn't know the exact date of any conscription order, but I'm sure that may be right. My experience in Sarajevo, which doesn't begin until a year after these events would indicate to me that there wasn't a 100 per cent response, but they did -- they did organise an army in the months that followed. And with regard to an earlier conversation we had about the political situation, that army included large numbers of -- of Serbs and Croats in what is called the Muslim side. I don't know what the take-up on the conscription was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we go to the next page, please. In the boxed part you say that there was no visible evidence of serious violence, let alone systematic extermination. Then you say that the Red Cross Yugoslav doctor stated that he had visited the location and that the detainees were in a good state save for a few cases of diarrhoea. Then you move on top Trnopolje; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. But the paragraph that says there's no visible evidence of serious violence means that we were seeing the people who were selected to come into the canteen, one of which did a minor wound to his face, actually, but we did not see any -- any very serious violence. But the point I'm making here and the bit that you have kindly boxed is that we were trying to get into the -- into the -- into the hangar, the shed, where -- well, I mustn't speak with hindsight, but where we had suspicions that appalling things were taking place. Hindsight has shown that they were, and what I'm trying to say in that paragraph that you have marked is that it was worth breaking your promise to stop us seeing them that day, and -- sorry. And now that I know what I know, what this Tribunal knows, I can see why, because what was happening in there was absolutely appalling and had been for three months. That's -- and then we go to Trnopolje. Yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you know what took place inside, and how do you know that the detainees to be shown to you were cherry picked? Let's not discuss your assessment. Do you know it for a fact?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how long Your Honours want to listen to what is my work over the years listening to other people. So I've heard from, as I said, scores of people who were in Omarska, that there was widespread and systematic killing and many of them lost family there in appalling circumstances. It's not for me to give the whole history of the camp unless you want it from me in terms of this -- these testimonies that I've taken over these years, but the Tribunal's own record over the years would, I think, suffice in the cases that I've testified in including Tadic, Stakic, and Kovacevic to give some idea of what was happening in that hangar and other buildings in the Omarska camp. I can elaborate on the interviews I've done, if you wish, but to summarise, I think we can say that your judgement that this was the worst prison is correct and that the most atrocious things were happening in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm just trying to ascertain something. What are the sources of your information? Are you relying completely on what has taken place before this Tribunal and your conversations with the Muslims and those who during the civil war fought the side that was in charge of the prison; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: My sources would be survivors of the camp, yes, some of whom testified to this Tribunal, many of whom have testified to this Tribunal on oath; international assessments that have been made; those bereaved by the hundreds of -- some of the hundreds of people who were bereaved by the murders in the camp. And in a way Dr. Kovacevic's remorse was a guide although the details are provided. But, yes, the main survivors over the years whose terrible experience that has been corroborated by a vast wealth of evidence here on oath at this Tribunal to mass murder, torture, beating, and rape. Sorry, I didn't answer an element in your question. With regard to the selection, I have heard from a number of survivors that on August the 4th, while we are on our way, large numbers of prisoners were taken out onto the Pista, as it's called, the tarmac area between the hangar and the canteen where these altercations in the film are taking place and a group selected for, as it were, presentation in the canteen, what was to be the following day, and that I've heard it from large numbers of people that they were judged to be those that were in better condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, do you know that people were taken out to the pista daily to get some fresh air, not only when you arrived. It happened every day, and anyone who was not being interrogated at that moment was taken out to the pista to get some fresh air.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, that's not so much a question as an assertion. And it seems -- I only speak for myself, of course, but it seems to me that this is a topic that one could go on and on about ad infinitum without it really relating to the essence of this witness's testimony. You may agree with that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, Your Excellency. It is a fact, however, that the witness said the detainees were taken out to the pista for their sake and that only 80 of them who were in better condition were chosen. I simply wished to remind the witness that the taking out of prisoners in that way to the pista happened daily, not only on that occasion. In any case, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You go on in your book -- could we go down to the bottom of the page. You say that a group arrived from Keraterm. Did you try and verify whether 200 people were indeed killed at Keraterm and all those perhaps in a single day and many more at Omarska? But you also say he has seen no bodies himself, but other people told him.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It was -- it was hard to try and verify on that day whether this alleged massacre had taken place in Keraterm, but -- and with hindsight, I know that now that particular day it's not 200. It's about 150. But that has been the subject of a -- of a trial at this Tribunal since, and I was happy to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I was convinced enough to quote this boy at the time that -- that he says 200 were killed at Keraterm and many more at Omarska, and I did quote him, and I think hindsight will show and the proceedings of this Tribunal have shown that although he got the number wrong at Keraterm, the -- the massacre did take place and many more were certainly killed at Omarska. He's telling the truth, essentially.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, he was not at Omarska. He was in Keraterm, and he didn't see any bodies there either; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: He was among the group that had come from Keraterm and Omarska that morning that we saw in the picture. On the day, yes, he is -- I am quoting someone who is quoting maybe people he knew who had arrived from Omarska that day, but knowing what I know now, I'm happy to have reported that -- that he said many more people had been killed at Omarska. Whether he means many more than 200, I don't know, but many more than 200 were killed at Omarska, so he's telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I told you, Mr. Vulliamy, that none of it is true and that all those who said anything about killings saw a single killing of a person who was mentally disturbed, would you believe me or would you believe them? And why do you choose their stories, although you say that the boy didn't see any bodies but someone else did, and he was never at Omarska? It seems you choose to believe things which are to the detriment of the Serbs quite easily, lightly.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't choose to believe things that are detrimental to one side or the other. I don't believe that only one person was killed in Omarska and Keraterm put together, and I do believe this -- what this boy says when he talked about -- although, as I said, the number on that day is not 200, so far as I know, that I do believe that -- that very many more than one single mentally disturbed person was killed in the combination of Omarska and Trnopolje -- sorry, Omarska and Keraterm. So with respect, I have to say that if you tell me it's only one, I don't believe you, sir. Nothing personal. I just heard differently from so many places and sources and people, including people testifying on oath at this Tribunal, whose testimony has been upheld in a number of cases. And the detriment to the Serbs is irrelevant. That's not how I measure these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, it would be irrelevant if it were true. However, I told you that they all saw a single killing. They all discussed killings but saw only one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, you're making an assertion as to matters which are evidential. This is not a proper question in cross-examination. You've made the point that you don't accept the witness's findings. It's not going to be improved by argument, and in terms of the time limitations, it's certainly my view, I don't know if it's the view of my colleagues, that you ought to move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. I was imprecise. I was addressing what the witness said when he stated that I claim that there was only one killing, but it was actually what the people were saying and saw. It is my position that they all discussed it but no one saw more than one killing. You also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Briefly only. You believed that Trnopolje could not be termed a concentration camp.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we turn on to the next page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was that a question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wanted to show something else about Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You believed that Trnopolje was not a concentration camp and that some people arrived there voluntarily as they were fleeing combat which took place in the vicinity of their villages; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Sorry, yes and no. The usage of the term "concentration camp" I can discuss now separately as the -- as Your Honours wish. As regards fleeing combat which took place in the vicinity, no. Trnopolje was a complicated place. Some people had been corralled there from their villages. Others had gone there, as you said in your interview with us, because their villages had been burned down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As to the term "concentration camp," I thought Mr. Karadzic was citing your article on the previous page. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On the previous page. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, just below the last box.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, you spotted that correctly. Thank you. Could we go back to the next page then. We see here that you state very professionally that there was no compulsion and that the conditions were simply that of being hot and that there was some stench. There seems to be a person there saying that he was a fighter and that they put them in front themselves. He was so terrified and fled to the Serbian side of the village. He was still in fear and felt safer in Trnopolje. Then just below you say that he arrived from Rizvanovici after the fighting. He also says that the Muslim side initiated the fighting and that the police arrived and took the people away in order to -- to cleanse the village and to do the fighting. Mr. Vulliamy, you noted quite professionally the sentences which corroborate in full the position of this Defence; is that correct? Is this what the people told you? You didn't just make it up, did you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No. I'm -- here's -- here's a boy who gets caught, and there is shooting from the Muslim side. The -- the -- the militias -- the Serbian militia's arrived to clear the village of Muslims and he's -- appears to have been caught in the crossfire. He's safer behind the lines of the advancing Serbs and he ends up in Trnopolje. I think, Your Honours, I came across -- I came across that day and have come across so many different reasons why people were in Trnopolje, and this term "concentration camp" is -- is -- it's a definition we can go into if you want. I don't dispute what Dr. Karadzic says. He is a boy who is caught in crossfire and has -- want -- and is better off there than in his village which has been cleared of his people, and there has been shooting to achieve that. And I'm not disputing that there was not -- I'm sorry. I'm not disputing that there was not shooting from the Muslim side, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were free to discuss things with them without the presence of guards; correct? And you could walk around at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: In some places, yes; in others, no. In the compound that we saw behind the fence, the people from Omarska and Keraterm, no. The conversations in the medical centre, if it can be called that, I don't want the Bench to think this was some sort of clinic. It was the room where these two people were doing their desperate best. We were supervised as the interview with Mr. Merdzanic makes clear. And in other points, yes, you are correct, I was able to walk around on my own and with somebody who I found who spoke English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, Judge Baird.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Is it possible for you to give us, as briefly as possible, some idea as to what you deemed a camp, concentration camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you. If I could just explain. The day that my story was published, August the 7th, 1992, I did this sort of fairly absurd number of some 50 something radio interviews, television interviews, and time after time invocations were made of the Holocaust, and Auschwitz and Birkenau. This is in itself a long subject that I won't trouble you with now, but I felt that at the time, and I think there were, and I have consulted authorities at Holocaust museum and so on, to try and find the language, and there were echos as authorised by them -- echos. Yes. But this is down the line. At the time, I felt that this invocation of the shoah was unhelpful, to be honest. We -- I was trying to talk about what we had seen, what we had found, what we feared we had not found, if you like, that headlines like "Belsen 1992" didn't really help. So I was disinclined to call, certainly, Trnopolje a concentration camp. This is all happening within a short space of time and fairly frantically. I have decided, as I say, after consultation with people in the Holocaust museum and survivors, to use the term but actually with -- very much with reference to its proper definition which comes from the Boer War in South Africa, and the more I've researched it, I think it's as fair to say that Trnopolje was camp, exactly that, where thousands of civilians were concentrated prior to enforced deportation of -- on the convoys of the kind that I accompanied across Mount Vlasic. So it's a discourse in itself, but that's the conclusion I've come to after the best consultations I can muster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The entire page is truly of interest and good, too. Could we please have a look at this. You saw that were Muslim villages that were intact, peasants calmly working. Every house was marked by a white flag, a piece of sheet, and that was their guarantee against Omarska or Trnopolje. And then Colonel Milutinovic explained to you that they had accepted Republika Srpska and then they were left alone; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he told us and, unfortunately, I believed him, because I now know that the sheets meant that you had agreed to leave. But at the time that's what he told me, and I believed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Says who? Who told you that? Who told you that that meant that they were supposed to leave, when the Muslims themselves say clearly that they had been told whoever doesn't want to fight can put this marking on their house so that we should not have any fear of that house, that we should not fire at that house. Who said that to you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The people who hung the sheets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, we did agree during our interview that in a civil war like that the two sides tried to blacken each other, as it were. In your view, how many Muslim were is killed in this war? You are relying on what the media said and what was in the public domain. How many Muslims were victims in this war?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't have the figures to hand, but there is a report by two investigators who -- who -- who gave a paper to a conference in Berlin, and they -- what they did was they sort of combined the work of ICRC, International Commission for Missing Persons, both the commissions of the various entities, and they come up with I think -- and I need to confirm this in the break, if Your Honours will allow me, but it's something like I think it's -- I think it's 58.000 or so. That's the figure I know from memory. There are an enormous number of estimates. This is by two Polish experts. I can get the -- the names and the numbers, but as I recall, it's something like 58- or 59.000 Muslims killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you heard the figure of 250- to 300.000, which figured prominently throughout the war as the number of Muslims only that had fallen victim? Have you heard of this figure of 80.000 raped women?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I have heard the figure of 300.000 dead in the war which, as you say, is correctly prominent throughout the war. I now know that to be incorrect. It doesn't stand up forensically. Eighty thousand rapes -- raped women seems high. I have heard a figure of tens of thousands of women raped. Lower than 80, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that out of these 55 or 6 or 7.000 Muslims a number were killed as fighters?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I think on all -- on all three sides you have both military and civilian killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that about 35.000 Serbs lost their lives?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: That's not the figure in this report that -- that I -- that I'm quoting, and I don't know where that comes from. I -- I'm afraid I just haven't got these figures off the top of my head, but it's 20-something thousand Serbs. I think it's 21.000 in that report I'm citing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This article will be admitted as Exhibit D1898.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that both you and Ms. Marshall and her associate - actually, they stated that - realised only in Budapest when they saw their footage from Trnopolje on TV, they realised that that was a big story, as it were, when they saw that President Bush, Sr., interfered with his comment?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I can't speak for Ms. Markale or Mr. Williams when they got to Budapest, but I think I am -- a big story. Important, I'd rather say. We talked about this yesterday. I think I realised that as soon as I walked into the canteen in Omarska and saw those men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 1D4825. Could we have a look at that. We should disregard what it says in Serbian. These are my notes. This is some conversation, or maybe it was a talk show, or maybe it was live. These are yours words and the words of Ms. Marshall. Actually, do you know when you stated this?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly which interview. I'm just reading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The next page. Could we have that, please? On the top here you say that you returned yet again, and further down we see that you returned to Omarska. Can we have a look further down where you say -- actually, President Bush spoke about this, and you say that you were on the phone all day, and you even say down here: [In English] [As read] "These people were all skin and bone, really gaunt and -- in terrible -- these men were emaciated grotesquely, undernourished and thin, bony, gaunt, wiry ...," and so on. [Interpretation] How come this is not contained in your first report? How come it's there when it became a big story?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Can we get the first report back up again, because I think I do talk about states of decay and emaciation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We don't have enough time. The participants have this before them, and I can give you a copy, but we just don't have time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We upload Exhibit D1898.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fact that's -- Mr. Vulliamy's article is an associated exhibit, so it would be having a Prosecution exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It's 1D4821 is already admitted as associate exhibit, is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It should have an exhibit number shortly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As regards -- sorry, to answer your question, as regards this silly remark about number 1 for -- I mean, it was a crazy day. I'm not someone who likes to, you know, bob up on the media all the time on other people's progress.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us show the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Young man, emaciated, sunken-eyed, attacking watery bean stew like a famished dog" -- it's a bit over -- I mean, it's what it is. "Spindly hands shaking." It is what it is. Yeah, I dont see any great discrepancy between that description and what I said, you know -- yet another of these interviews. I can't remember exactly which one it was. President Bush was -- it was completely irrelevant to what I was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Internees, horribly thin, raw-boned, some with almost cadaverous, with skin-like parchment folded around their arms, faces, lantern-jawed, eyes haunt by the empty stare of the prisoner," et cetera. So I think, in reply to your question, I would say that I had -- while I was writing that, talking to nobody on August the 6th, for publication on the 7th, when I presume that interview was recorded is one of very many. I think I probably got the gist, from what I saw, of what condition these men were in rather than taking any cue from the President of the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go back to the previous document now, 1D4825. Could we have the last page. Are you talking about how hungry the public was for stories about Belsen and things like that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I just read what he -- the text. Yes. This is a reference to what I was trying to explain to the Bench in -- in one of Your Honour's queries about this -- this automatic parallel that was being made between what we had found and the Holocaust, which I considered to be unuseful at the time and certainly in need of -- of careful refinement before we started jumping into all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1899, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you were in Prijedor, all the local leaders were ready to see you and talk to you; right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. They made it clear that they didn't -- that it was reluctant. Mr. Kovacevic said, "I'm against this visit," even though you are welcome or something to that effect, but they agreed to see us, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During that group meeting, did you get an impression as to who was in charge and who issued orders to who?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic was introduced as the -- sorry, I didn't know he was doctor then. Milomir Stakic was introduced as the president; Kovacevic, the vice-president. Kovacevic did most of the talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also they informed you about the problems that the authorities had about the misdeeds that had been committed against the Serbs; right? You spoke about that what you testified in Stakic, 1998, 15th of July, pages 787 and 778; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Again, Kovacevic, I take it, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've described the meeting in both -- both those trials, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. They informed you about Hambarine there. They informed you about the torturing of children, and Kovacevic told you that he, as a child, had been a prisoner at the Jasenovac camp; right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, they did talk about fighting in Hambarine, and they showed us a video about what they called a jihad in the area, and certainly Kovacevic, to my recollection, said that he had been born in Jasenovac, which when I went to revisit him he said that he had been taken there as a child, but he had certainly been in that appalling place, so he said, and I believed him, and still do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in your testimony in Kovacevic, on page 795, I'll read it in English: [In English] "On their way to Omarska, they were attacked and they were told that it was ..." [Interpretation] Actually you described that. You said that you were attacked and you were told that it was the Mujahedin, and you said that all this had been rigged and you repeated that today as well. How come you were sure of that and what would that mean to us?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: What convinced me was, first of all, how the shots were going over our heads high, and anyone who was trying to shoot at us clearly not very good. The return of fire was also high, and then when it sort of -- when we said this is ridiculous let's carry on, and it's -- it stopped so suddenly and we carried on, it didn't feel like a -- a proper ambush from the experience that I had of the war in Croatia and previously in Iraq.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And it never crossed your mind that they were firing at one another and that they were not targeting you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: If they were, they were rotten shots. Sorry, I don't mean to be facetious. It might have done for a moment, but not after a while. I -- I thought it was a prank then, and I still do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So whatever the Serbs say, that will be your view; isn't that right, Mr. Vulliamy? During the interview, I informed you that the Serbs consider you to be highly partial, most partial; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, if so, that's unfortunate. I am, as I tried to explain in -- when we were talking about neutrality, I am highly partial about extreme violence. I'm not highly partial about any particular race of people or -- or -- or ethnicity or whatever. In fact, I'm highly partial against racialism. So I'm not anti-Serb. I'm anti-what was done. In name, sometimes, of Serbia, tragically, which was opposed by very large number of Serbs at the time and since. And if Their Honours want to hear about my social acquaintances with Serbs, I'm very welcome to supply it. I don't want to sound like some of my best friends are but my colleague with whom I worked during the year of the war described in the book is a Serb and I knew many Serbs during the war and still know many now, so I'll leave my answer at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned today that as far as Trnopolje was concerned, it was a camp for deportees. During the interview, we established that you did know that people could leave and get food; right? During the interview, you said that some could and others couldn't. This is what I'm putting to you now as well: People who had their own vegetable gardens could go and get food, and probably the people who did not have their own gardens did not go to get food because there was no other way of getting food. What was it that you knew?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: What -- the -- who could and couldn't leave Trnopolje seems to be quite capricious. Obviously if you were from Prijedor, which is a long way away, you wouldn't be going home, and some people were forcibly brought there. Others went of their own accord, and we've established that. I don't know exactly who was able to leave and who wasn't. I know that it had to be negotiated. I've spoken to people at the medical centre. They were able to get people who were abandoned in their houses, infirm or whatever, and were brought to Trnopolje. Others were corralled on buses, as is well established by this Tribunal, were taken there en masse. So -- and this is why it's -- the definition has been an issue, and I decided to call it a concentration camp on the basis of the South Africa dictionary definition. But your point about who was and wasn't allowed to leave to get food and who was or wasn't allowed to so under guard is whimsical. I don't exactly understand what the rules were if there were any hard and fast rules. I'd just like to, if I may, if Your Honours will allow me to get back to this point about this serious allegation of extreme partiality, it is in the record, but I proceeded immediately after all this to go and look at -- investigate camps with Serbian prisoners and I think I'm the only person who actually uncovered them. Sorry, I'm retrogressing there, but I do take this sort of allegation of anti-Serbian sentiment extremely seriously and I'd like to go on to -- if I'm asked about that visit to the camp, which I may not be, I'd just like to put it on record that I -- I made it my business to do exactly that. In fact, it was a camp that Mr. Karadzic on the film that we saw, it's one of those that he wanted to go and see, and I made it my business to do so in the interests of impartiality, and partiality over the practise of putting people into camps. So it was Serbian prisoners in the other one. Sorry, I'm replying to the previous question. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm not smiling at you. I am smiling with you. I anticipate I would be doing much the same thing. For this reason, as you know, Dr. Karadzic, it's been said in open court many times and I say it again, it isn't the Serbian people who are indicted in this case nor the Serbian state. It's you, and you need to concentrate on that reality.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency. However, as things stand, I have been indicted as the civilian head of state and of the army for everything that every crook did on the ground. I am trying to prove that this had nothing to do with the system whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, today you said, Mr. Witness, that they were brought after raids, but look at page 3 of this report of yours. This boy from Rizvanovic is telling you nicely. When the fighting started, the Serbs rallied the civilians and took them away so that they could continue the fighting. Do you know that in accordance with our law civilians have to be evacuated from a combat zone?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, and the civilians were evacuated from their homes and taken to Trnopolje and I don't know what exactly happened to the -- the civilians from that village, but I would be surprised if any of them had got back to their houses before about 1999, if at all. But I don't dispute what you're saying and what I wrote about this boy. Obviously it appears caught in the line of fire and as the village was, as the article says, cleared and taking refuge with -- with soldiers under your command and going to Trnopolje. I don't dispute that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for this deportation, do you know that these persons who after the Muslim extremists, the Green Berets, the Muslim extremists turned Prijedor into a theatre of war through their own actions, do you know that they asked to be evacuated either to Central Bosnia or to Europe, that they obtained many documents, that they paid for them? So that was not deportation. The Defence says that that was not deportation. This was evacuation, of course due to difficulties. However, it was based on requests made by these persons.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I didn't know that, no, because when I went with the people on that convoy, they told me something different, that -- that -- that soldiers and policemen had come around to their houses and given them ultimata to leave and sometimes they had some squabble over who was going to get the house and that they had been corralled, in this case, into a location in the village of -- town, sorry, of Sanski Most, and that the -- the people on the convoy that I travelled with were leaving anything but voluntarily. The convoy was marshalled to order by armed guards and patrolled along its way by armed guards. Nobody I spoke to had any idea where -- where they were going. Correction. Some people did know later, that I talked to later in the night when we were on foot, that they were going to -- to government-held territory. But I didn't meet anybody who gave me that account nor have I since spoken to anyone who has given me that account for what I did not know that night of August the 17th, 1992, but soon after knew when nightly deportation convoys, and indeed four nights after ours on August the 17th. There was one on August the 21st [Realtime transcript read in error "24th"] during which large numbers of people were taken off the buses and executed on Mount Vlasic, so -- known to this Tribunal as the Vlasic massacre. So, no, sir, I didn't know that those were the reasons why those convoys were going over Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we'll take a break now for half an hour. We will resume at half past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, very quickly. Back on page 64, I said that the Vulliamy article that was published on the 7th of August was an associated exhibit, and it is -- it is P3788. Correct me if I am wrong, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which is 65 ter number 19682.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And that was the "Guardian" article, whereas Mr. Karadzic has been using a copy of that article from the "Toronto Star" and has -- had certain -- taken the witness to certain boxes in that article so I think it's perhaps better that we keep a Prosecution and Defence exhibit unless Your Honours are minded to -- to cross-reference both in e-court perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we just leave it as it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I was suggesting, Your Honour. I'm sorry if I wasn't clear. And the other thing, just for the record so that it's clear, the interview that Mr. Karadzic keeps referring to that -- that the witness has had with him is an interview that was conducted yesterday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D04816 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, I would kindly ask you to just answer by yes or no whenever possible, because we don't have that much time, and secondly, please do not rely on what you have heard in this court or elsewhere, from somebody else. Just share with us what you know yourself. This is the most important thing for us here. Do you remember this text?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at the subtitle. It says that: "Ed Vulliamy is one of only two journalists to take the stand in the historic Bosnia war crimes trial at The Hague." Right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I wouldn't have written that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The way Mr. Karadzic put the question was that you took side -- sides with somebody. [In English] "He describes his day in court as witness for the Prosecution confronting an alleged torturer.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: That's what's called a stand first. I wouldn't have written it, but I was a witness for the Prosecution, yes. Your Honours, I've spotted quite an important error further up the transcript. I don't know what to do about that. Sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Our usher could assist you. I'm not sure whether your monitor can have that scroll. No. If you remember some word that we can find it, I will read it to you so that you can correct it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sorry. Yes, this is a stand first. I wouldn't have written it but it does say accurately, sir, that I testified for the Prosecution, which I did. I think this is the Tadic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now you can scroll. I think you can find the text you have in mind. Could you took -- take a look.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- sorry, Your Honours. It's just before we went for the break there are dates and things that are wrong. Our convoy was August the 17th, 1992, and the massacre was four days after ours on August the -- ours was on the 17th. The massacre was on the 21st, not the 24th. I do apologise for interrupting. Sorry, Dr. Karadzic for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Four days after ours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Four days after. Ours is on the 17th, not the 18th, and the massacre is on the 21st.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise to Your Honours and Dr. Karadzic for spoiling the -- interrupting the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not at all. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you this: You said that there was police escort. Do you know that on the 22nd of May we signed a commitment to escort civilians who were transferring from one side to the other? Just yes or no. In other words, UNHCR was a middle man and the three sides signed an agreement for the police to escort all civilian convoys crossing from one side to the other.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about this agreement, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go to the following page, please. Let's look at the second paragraph at the bottom above the advert. Yes, this is it. There is a reference here to Dr. Azra Blazevic. You mentioned her yourself earlier today. It is also stated that Trnopolje camp is a concentration camp; right? A bit further up there is a reference to Omarska and the other camps in the Serbian gulag. Do you see that? We have lost it now. Can we scope up a little. Scroll up. The second column. Scroll down, scroll down. Very well, now that's it. Yes. There's a reference to Omarska: [In English] "In the other camps in Serbia's gulag, and --" [Interpretation] It says here that Trnopolje's a concentration camp just after the reference is being made to Dr. Azra Blazevic; right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the far right end of the document. Here you are quoted as saying [In English] I would have been as proud to testify --" no, no, no, no, no. "... to testify for Sir Hartley against the Nazis as I am to do so at The Hague against those who echoed them with a pale but unmistakable imitation." [Interpretation] Is it your view indeed that we are a pale but unmistakable imitation of the Nazis?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I'll stand by that. We discussed this. Indeed it's a point of semantics and a point of history. The word "echo" I -- was, what was it, forged, if you like, the right to use that word in consultation with people at the Holocaust Memorial Museum in Washington. Pale, yes. Unmistakable, yes. And again, it's -- we're back to this point about the internment, murder of people for reasons of ethnicity, mass deportation for reasons of ethnicity, and so, yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: -- I will stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. We've already heard that and we don't have time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if you ask the question, you should allow the witness to complete his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I apologise. I believe that the side questioning the witness should control them. If I had the time, I would only be too glad to listen to Mr. Vulliamy, but if not, then I just wanted to know whether this is Mr. Vulliamy's view or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, my next question is this: Do you now think that this contributed to the fact that some Serbs consider you as having anti-Serb views?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, if some do, then perhaps they're the ones who support what was being done in their name. The Serbian friends that I have and have had throughout -- throughout the war and still have do not, and many of them, I think, would probably agree with this -- with this estimation. There are -- if we're going to continue with this echo, there are very large numbers of Germans who were appalled by what was done in their name and have been part of the reckoning in that country to -- to come to terms with it. If any Serb thinks I'm against all Serbs, they are, A, wrong, and I regret that they held that view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1900, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to show you an exhibit, a Prosecution exhibit, an excerpt from a visit to Trnopolje. You know very well the dispute that broke out between the "Living Marxism" where Thomas Deichmann published that that was staged. And now I'm going to show you that the wire that is depict -- depicted actually the wire surrounding building tools protected them and not the people who were detained in Trnopolje. 4504. 65 ter 40504, and the English transcript page is 6. No, no, not that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we stop here? Do you see any wire here, Mr. Vulliamy, or are these people seated in a totally open area?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I -- it's hard -- I can't see any wire, and I don't know whether this was shot on August the 5th or when the -- as I called it, the circus went back by which time the wire had come down, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now we will see. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is just one part. Do you agree -- we will see that that was taken on the same day when you and Penny Marshall were there, the same journalist. Everything is the same.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: That last picture, yes, sir, that appears to be August the 5th. I think we've seen an excerpt from that before. That's when we were there, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And please bear with me while I'm looking for the number of that excerpt where you will also see Mr. Bozanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can -- if Mr. Karadzic is wanting the exhibit number of that excerpted, it's P03697.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you very much. I would like to call that up, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, this isn't --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to go back to the beginning. This is not the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is -- this is still taken from the -- this footage that was just played is coming from the bigger video-tape. I thought Mr. Karadzic just wanted the excerpt that was shown through a witness last week or just very recently that was admitted through him, and that is Exhibit P03697 and it's 65 ter number 40504B. It's a 15-second clip.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's -- that's precisely that. I apologise for not being precise enough. 40504B. Can we see that? Do we have it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What I was told is that we -- e-court has the transcript but not the -- not the video itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, this morning I played that -- I played that excerpt this morning. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Reid.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Reid is getting it in Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Our thesis which was also proposed by Mr. Deichmann that the fence around the compound with building tools is what we saw and that Ms. Marshall entered the compound and that she was on the other side within the wire and not the detainees. You in your turn contest that; right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This thesis, as you call it, was advanced in 1996 or 1997. We'd heard nothing of it in between 1992 and that year from you or anybody else. And I do contest it, yes. I am, if anything, more convinced now than I was even on that day that those men were detained and under guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How come you are more convinced today than when you saw things with your own two eyes. What is it that makes you more convinced today than ever before?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, at the time, it was very obvious to me that they were prisoners, but since then, as you know and the Bench may know, there has been a court case in London -- when you mentioned "Living Marxism" who published this thesis, your word, were sued by ITN and lost. ITN won the case. It was a civil case, I agree, at lower burden of proof, and I had the opportunity to interview a number of the prisoners since who have described to me how they got there, why they were there, and they were certainly -- we were not filming -- they were not filming, sorry, from inside any compound outside, nor was I, let's talk about me, not ITN, interviewing people through that fence from inside any kind of detention facility taking notes from people who were at liberty wandering around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You derive the additional information from the events and developments at various courts and you tend to believe that information more than you believe what you saw with your own two eyes; right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No. I believed what I saw with my own two eyes that they were prisoners and were detained and under guard behind that fence and others, and on talking to them I have that belief confirmed and this has been gone over and over on oath many times, and -- I'm not saying especially more -- I'm saying that my description of them as prisoners has been proved accurate over and over again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The video-clip's ready, if Mr. Karadzic wishes to play it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I stop here, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, do you see a single emaciated person like that person Alic was?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Not in this picture, no. They were in various states of decay I think was the word I used. But I'm -- I'm -- I'm saying they're prisoners. No, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we continue. [Video-clip played] 6c

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see the tools here? Do you see that this is actually a storage of all the building tools and equipment? Do you see the wheelbarrows and things like that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I can see wheelbarrows by the fence, yes. I didn't notice them at the time. There were other things to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you at the time notice and did you make a note of what you noticed, and that was that the fourth side did not have any wire, that it was open?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: To my recollection, the compound was wire on three sides and a building on the fourth side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 1D04818 is what would I like to call up now. 1D04818. Do you remember that you were interviewed by Slobodna Bosna on the 10th of August, 1997? The title here is "I live for the day when I'm going to take a stand in The Hague against Karadzic."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't remember doing that interview. I don't deny that I did it, and I take no responsibility for the headline they put on it. No disrespect. I have not lived for this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see the next page, please. It seems that you also had to say something about Minister Douglas Hurd. Can we also see the following page in Serbian, and now we can see the title here, "How did Karadzic make a mistake?" The question here is: How come you were invited to visit the camps? And you say that while you were in London, Karadzic invited me to see Omarska, Manjaca, and Trnopolje, and so on and so forth. The next question is about the permit that you received to visit those camps. Why do you think that Karadzic allowed you to visit the camps? He could have changed your mind. And your answer is: God knows. My assumption is that he did not intend to let us see Omarska. We know that because there was a prank set up for us in the form of a false battle, and our escorts told us that those were Mujahedin in the forest. We demanded that we should continue. The Red Cross was already in Manjaca. I suppose that he wanted to show us a small part of Trnopolje. He certainly didn't want us to see the part where people from Keraterm and Omarska were brought or else Karadzic is as stupid as happens [as interpreted]. After all, he was the last one to laugh, right, and so on and so forth. Wouldn't you say that this is another thing that has prompted some Serbs to believe that you are impartial and that you will not be an objective witness in my trial? Things have not been recorded properly. You said "or else Karadzic is as stupid as he appears." This is what you said, and this was not recorded. This interview of yours, did it contribute or did it provide the basis for people's concerns and doubts about your impartiality as a witness in -- in my trial?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I'd like to, in response to many questions there, first of all, establish some distance between what I say and what appears in Bosnian magazines. I haven't had this translated back to me before, but I have had other articles translated back to me which -- and I do not recognise what I said. I would just like to put it on record that whatever else I might think about what had happened under your authority, I do not think you're stupid, sir. I have actually said to a number of people over the last 48 hours that you are clever and I would like that put on record. As regards the other matters, yes, I was and remained curious and sometimes baffled as to why you did authorise the visit to Omarska. What I suppose I was trying to explain to this magazine is that when we got there, judging from what we were told and what happened and our inability to see inside the hangar, that, as it was put by Mrs. Balaban earlier in evidence, we could see this and this and that but not that. And he quotes her again. He promised us something else. So I suppose what I was trying to convey to them was that perhaps you had intended us to see one part of the camp and not the other. That was my inference from what Mrs. Balaban was saying. With regard to Trnopolje, and I'm inferring here, I -- perhaps you did think that it would be all right for us to see the main area with the buildings and the -- where the medical centres were but perhaps could not have anticipated our coming upon the men who were in that compound who had that day, August the 5th, arrived from Omarska and Keraterm, but I would like to use this opportunity to retract and perhaps to rebuke this magazine for translating me as calling you stupid because I do not think you're stupid and I never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Why do you presume so much when I openly told you you could see everything for yourselves? Yet you revert to your presumptions again trying to guess what my intention was. My intention was for you to go and see it all and to make sure that the people in the field will -- were aware of the fact that someone was going to see it. Why do you back to presumptions?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I suppose because they're not presumptions. They're based on -- just on what we were told when we went in there. When we tried to cross the tarmac pista to go into the hangar, we were told that you -- we were, sorry. We were told, I was told - I can't say I -- I was told -- I was standing behind Ms. Marshall at the time that you had told them we couldn't and, as I think is clear from the film, so that's the basis of what you call my presumption. I wish you had -- we had been allowed to -- I -- I don't know what your exact instructions to them were because I wasn't privy to them, but my understanding was that we would see everything and we didn't see everything. In fact, we hardly -- we saw the tip of the iceberg but it was explained to us that your authority did not extend to us seeing all the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday when we met, we discussed Mr. Williams having conveyed something and you overheard that. Supposedly someone said that my instructions are not abided by there, and in the interview I repeated my words when I said that if there were people there who were disobedient, I'd be most interested in seeing who they were.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I recall us looking at Mr. Williams's remarks on paper and his inference was that your -- hang on. His inference in the transcript that we looked at was that your authority didn't, as I think you put it, carry weight in Omarska but this is between -- this is for Mr. Williams to -- to talk about. What I understood was that what was being explained was that we had been told that we would be able to see that the camp, indeed the whole region, unfettered and it turned out that we were fettered, and it was explained to me, us, that -- that that was not the case, that your instruction were, as Mrs. Balaban translated, otherwise. What Mr. Williams made of that, you'd better call him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But Mr. Williams quoted someone else, a local Serb. Apparently he was told that Karadzic's instructions or orders do not carry weight there. He was quoting someone. It wasn't his conclusion, was it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I didn't hear those words being used by anybody else, but -- but I was dependent on -- on -- because I don't understand the language, I was dependent on what Mrs. Balaban was saying, which we've seen part of it. A relevant part of which was -- and again I don't recall the exact words but that -- I think he says he promised us something else and that we could see this and this but not that. That there was a dichotomy between our understanding -- our respective understandings on what you had authorised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that on page 15, line 21, we have her words incorrectly interpreted. She only said, "I was only there to interpret." She wasn't interpreting my words. She simply placed a hedge protecting herself having said I'm here only to interpret.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't infer that she was making the decisions herself. My inference, as she was interpreting as she said, was that the -- as it were the block on our further visiting and going into the part of the camp that I now understand to be the bit that mattered was being imposed by Mr. Drljaca, Colonel Milutinovic, and Mr. Meakic who would have been in a position of authority, not her. As she said, she was translating for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this interview be admitted. Unfortunately, only this column was translated. If necessary, we could have it all translated, although I don't see the need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Original is four pages and the translation is three pages. I think that's sufficient, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will, ourselves, take a -- review this article in B/C/S and bring anything to your attention that we need to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we can admit only those part then which has been translated.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. At the moment, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1901, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I briefly wanted you to see what the deportations in question looked like. For that purpose, could we see 1D4820. Of course when it refers to me deportation is in inverted commas. Please have a look at this article, interview with an official of the Red Cross. It was in Banja Luka, and the Red Cross director said Muslims must be moved. The entire interview, have a look at the fourth paragraph, for instance, says that there are people who wished to leave and there were between 1- and 200.000 alone in this region around Banja Luka. It goes on to say even if we were to find a solution now for these 3- or 4.000 people, we would immediately have to deal with 10.000 who would follow, and so on and so forth. Did you know of this position taken by the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I've had various altercations with the Red Cross over their handling of the camps. I didn't know about this particular position but it doesn't surprise me. The word desperately strikes me in this text, but I -- this is a conversation between -- someone called Jakovsky and someone called Schweizen. I can't really comment on it. I have to read it to know exactly what they're saying. I take it this is the Red Cross -- as I understand it, this is the Red Cross, but I don't know if it's the ICRC or the local Red Cross saying that people are desperate to leave. What I do have direct experience of is a deportation convoy and I can testify to that if -- if Your Honours want me to or if you ask me about it. And certainly none of these people asked to leave, quite the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We can go back to the top. It appears to be the director of the ICRC who was in Banja Luka at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the document admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If Mr. Robinson can help us on what basis we should admit this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, frankly, Mr. President, I don't see any basis on which you can admit it, based on what the witness has testified to so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you'll have another opportunity to tender that through another witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have 1D04817, please. Please zoom in on the bottom half.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your commentary concerning the arrest of Saddam Hussein? And there is a reference to me.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have any proof that I was a tyrant?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Can we just -- sorry, sir, to answer your question, no. No, I'm aware that you were elected by your party, though not in -- though not in -- not in the Presidency with regard to the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do I use the term "tyrant" in the copy? Because can we just -- the thing is I wouldn't have written the headline.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe so. Could we go to the next page. Look at the paragraph beginning with "Imagine Radovan Karadzic."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your position about me?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Forgive the cocksure swagger. You did have one at the time. The language is a little strong, I'll admit, but I don't see me describe you as a tyrant. I'm aware that you were elected. Rhetoric, yes. Bloodlust, I'm not sure about you personally but certainly in your name. And I was not particularly gratified by the site of the stuck [indiscernible] as much as I despised him. I'll grant you the language is a little strong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the bottom: [In English] "There will be no Guantanamo Bay for the camp guards of Omarska or the execution at Srebrenica." [Interpretation] Can we go to the next page then. [In English] "For three years --" [Interpretation] Have a look at that paragraph: [In English] "For three years the great powers wined and dinned Karadzic, flattering this tin-pot tyrant's delusions of statesmanship."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Right. Well, you have that. I called you a tin-pot tyrant. And the point is that this is actually directed not so much as you as at the people in the West who I saw as, indeed, wining and dining you and shaking your hand under the chandeliers. Those of us working on the ground found this fairly baffling and much of -- many of those people were, after you were indicted, bayed for you to be arrested as a war criminal. As for the how Karadzic must have laughed to himself, I now know that from interviewing several of your entourage and friends in Belgrade, Pale and Sokolac and elsewhere that you did indeed find it, or at least they did -- and describe you finding it, yeah, fairly amusing that you were being feted in this way and that they took your -- that they took your -- I mean -- I -- I talk about tin-pot statesmanship. That's a little arrogant, I agree, but that -- that you were -- that I -- it has been described to me that you are -- found the seriousness with which you were being taken by these people very flattering, but that's hearsay again. These are your -- your entourage. No, they not in your garage, they're your entourage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Do you know that Mr. Akashi was on the Muslim's blacklist because he addressed his letter to me as His Excellency, as I did to him? Do you know he ended up on their blacklist for that? And does it reconcile with the position you express?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Sorry. No, I didn't know he was on any particular blacklist. I personally found his -- if Your Honours will accept political discourse, diplomatic assessments, I found his tolerance of what was going on for these three long bloody years -- I didn't agree with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
