utterances.text: Do you agree that Mr. Akashi must have been more familiar with the reasons of the conflict than you were because he dealt with all four warring parties? He was in discussions with all of them.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: He listened to many more politicians and diplomats than I did. I didn't talk to many of either, but he saw a lot less of what was happening on the ground than I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have this admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1902, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D4805.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this another text of yours from 2010?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your commentary of my introductory remarks or my opening statement, rather, when the trial began?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page please. Have a look at the second paragraph. [In English] "Karadzic's arguments," and so on. [Interpretation] And the third paragraph I won't read them all. Could this have contributed to the Serb belief that you are not biased, that you see things to our detriment?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It depends who we are. Serbian -- it's -- it's not for me to second-guess what Serbian people think, but what I'm saying here is that this continual denial and revision, to use the term of -- of what happened in those camps and the existence of the camps, has a searing effect on those who survive them and were bereaved by them and that's the point I'm making in -- in the penultimate picture -- at paragraph, sorry. But the -- with regard to what Serbs think about me, I would suppose answer that Serbs who supported what happened and who approve of what happened in those camps might dislike me and feel I was attacking them for -- for objecting to this grotesque notion that the camps were in some way fabricated by me and others but that those who disapprove of or never wanted anything to do with or indeed approved of but are now ashamed of such camps would have no reason to object to my objections to the notion that they were fabricated in an a media conspiracy because they were not. I hope that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But your position here is as if a judgement had already been pronounced. There isn't a single question mark. You simply appear to know things, and you assume your position; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I'm talking about here about -- sorry, it starts "invoke today" that I can see. I'm going certainly down that chain of command yourself, Dr. Koljevic, Milutinovic, Stakic, Kovacevic, et cetera, through the gates of the camp. That was seamless but this was about -- about the fake pictures argument that's been heard in this Tribunal many times. As I say here it's been destroyed by the Prosecution serially, run like a Basel through the internet. It does repeated in [indiscernible] it was. It is old. It goes back to 1996 but significantly not to 1992. It is tired because it keeps getting overthrown, and serially unsuccessful. But here, what I'm saying, sir, is it's heartless and poisonous because the people who advance it don't seem to imagine what it's like to survive or be bereaved by those camps and it has a terrible effect on them, this idea that somehow their suffering did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] could we have this admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for that, Mr. Vulliamy, I'll tell you this. The prisons for POWs were Kula, Batkovic and Manjaca. Omarska was an investigation centre. It was a factory, or rather, a mine which had to be brought to its original purpose. You, yourself, confirm that it was an investigation centre and that there were investigators working there around the clock in order to screen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that has been asked and answered. We'll admit that article as Exhibit D1903. Let us continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 1D04819 is the document that I would like to call up. 1D04819. While we're waiting, Mr. Vulliamy, could you please tell us how many interviews did you give? How many articles did you write after your visit to Omarska and Trnopolje? You said there were about 40 interviews; right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: That day, August the 7th, in Belgrade was endless interviews and I was not enjoying it, as I think I've indicated in print and in my testimony, and some of them annoyed me very much, but it was -- it was seen as something that people wanted to hear about. I don't know how many exactly. I think it was -- it must -- it was 40, 50. I mean, it was non-stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your book you say 54. How many article, how many texts you based on your visit? You say that there were about 200 or even 300 texts; right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't know how many, but I've written a lot about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we scroll up a little. You wrote this when I was arrested; right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your position in the article was clear. Again you were biased. Let me not read everything. You say that this was the first time after the Third Reich and you say that I arranged the mass murder of 100.000 people and the enforced deportation of 2 million people, and so on and so forth. Is this still your position even today?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It's for the Court to adjudicate whether you're directly responsible for it, but since that day we met and I went into the camps I can't deny that I haven't had a direct interest in it. It would be weird if it hadn't had an effect on my life. I have remained in touch with a large number of survivors and the bereaved, and I have been of the belief, again subject to the Court, that you were in a position of leadership over all this, as I say here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1904, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You received several coveted awards for journalism and for the results in writing of your visit to Omarska; right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I've specifically for that three or four, yes. Hang on. Four.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 1D04805 is the next document that I would like to call up. So we can say that this was the most productive ever visit to a place 54 interviews, hundreds of pages of articles and four coveted awards; right? No, that's not the document I want. We already saw that. Just a moment, bear with me. Do you agree that that was the most productive visit to anyplace during the war?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, I don't see it as productive. I would much rather have not found Omarska and as much as I did. Well, would -- 54 interviews would be irrelevant. I didn't enjoy any of them. I'm still on the same salary band as I was then. I am a working reporter. My pay has only increased incrementally. The awards mean a lot to some people, less to me, but I -- I'm -- I'm happy to have them. I have written another book and lost an awful lot of money in doing so. So, you know, it depends how one measures this word "productive." Do I wish that the world had never had Omarska in it? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, how much more do you have to conclude your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try and finish everything within the next 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have some re-examination, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: A few minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please do so in 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so, Your Honour, for witness scheduling can we excuse the witness that's waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think we're going to there -- going there --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- today. That's fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 1D4086 is the document number. This is your text, is it not, and this was written after General Mladic was arrested; right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. First, let's look at the photo. This person, Alic, does he appear to be joyful and happy? And what about the others? Do they appear to look differently than him? In other words, how can you be so certain that this is not just the way he normally looks, that this is not the way he is built but, rather, that he is emaciated?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: In all this I've heard that he's got TB, tuberculosis, which I know him not to have had. Sorry, what's the question? Do they appear to look different than him? Yes, but not from others inside the camp. And I -- I know that's not how he normally looks. I met him shortly -- well, I met him about ten months later and he looked very different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you saying that the TBC that broke out two months before, that, for example, if he -- his TBC had resulted from stress, from the fact that he was arrested, that his appearance could have deteriorated so much within the two months? If he didn't have TBC before he was arrested and if he contracted it on the day he was arrested, are you saying that within the two months his condition deteriorated so much that he was on the verge of extinction?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I -- yes, I would concede that perhaps the conditions in Keraterm were so appalling that his condition had deteriorated in two months and perhaps he had become sick there, but when I met him again in Slovenia the following spring, he was of a normal build. And he hadn't had much medical attention. He just had something to eat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you see him half naked when you saw him in Ljubljana also without his clothes on?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, he was clothed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] unfortunately, my figure is visible through my clothing, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And, now, look what you said here. You mentioned Dachau, and it doesn't really matter what you said about Dachau, there is a reference to Dachau in this text. Do you truly believe that this is unbiased journalism of the kind that makes you a good witness?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It is not up biased with regard to atrocities committed in concentration camps. It is not unbiased in terms of the neutrality that I tried to explain earlier. I think it is subjective in terms of facts and I stand by the argument in there which is an argument about people coming to terms with what is -- what has happened and what has been done. I am not unbiased over mass murder and beating and the kind of things that -- that are involved in these cases, but I am unbiased between peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On a condition that you were able to determine that there had been mass murder, did you establish it yourself or did you hear it from others and believed it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I've -- by the time I'd written this, which is recently, I had seen the exhumation of the mass graves, in particular the one at Kevljani which is just right next door to Omarska. I had been much in the Srebrenica area. I had met, I say, hundreds if not scores of people who had survived the camps and hundreds, if not scores, of people bereaved by the camps. And I have testified at and followed the proceedings of and the verdicts at this Tribunal. And I've been to the -- they're called the reassociation places where teams of forensic scientists and anthropologists and other experts are trying to put together the human remains from graves, secondary graves, and tertiary graves in an attempt to identify them and find their families. That's the basis on which I say that mass murder happened during this time in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you believe that people were also killed in combat, that a lot of people were killed in combat, as a matter of fact?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I do, without doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1905, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D4822 is the next document I would like to call up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is about your visits is to Mostar. Do you remember these texts as well?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Certainly I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the following page. You describe the conditions under which the Serbs were held by the HOS, and you identified the HOS as a pro-Nazi or a neo-Nazi organisation; right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's fair. The HOS was a mixed Croatian with some Muslim soldiers, and I think it's accurate to say that it was a neo-Ustasha militia and this was a camp run by them for Serbian prisoners.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1906, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now, please conclude in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In that case, I'm not going to show some documents. Let me ask you, you were engaged in some activities, and you looked at the conduct of both Serbs and Croats. Did you find the Muslim prisons that we talked about? For example, there were three in Sarajevo. Did you see any Muslim prisons for the Serbs? You can just say yes or no. No need to expand.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The prison at Dretelj, which is the one you're referring to, at Capljina, was run jointly by Croats and Muslims. I endeavoured to look at another site which you recommended, sir, to Tarcin, a tunnel and a silo, and they were empty at the time. I either was -- you know, failed to see prisoners if they were still there, I don't know, or they had been moved somewhere else. I wanted to get -- to do this -- this -- this -- this work on the other side, too, and proceeded straight to Capljina, which is the story you have there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In Sarajevo did you see any of the prisons that we talked about?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I -- I didn't actually go to the city itself of Sarajevo until well into 1993, by which time, and I don't mean to at all belittle the issue of camps, and I don't think I can be accused of that, there was another war going on in Mostar and in Central Bosnia in which your people, troops, whatever, were not involved, and I did not check out any -- any camps in the actual city of Sarajevo itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you observe the presence of Muslim troops? Let's call it the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the city did you also observe weapons, cannons, mortars, tanks?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: In the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the part of the city which was under Muslim control.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. SDA control, yes. It was -- it was ethnically mixed. Yes. I was up in the front lines there and did see the weaponry. I didn't see any artillery. A source of -- I saw that they had mortars, and they had guns in -- not in very -- not in very plentiful supply, but they -- they were equipped, yes, and became more so. By the -- 1994, they were better equipped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to ask you about the sources from which you learned things. Can it be said that most of your information came from Muslim sources? Is it true that you had a good exchange of information with the Red Cross, UNHCR, NGOs, and so on and so forth? Is all this correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Not -- not quite, sir. I mean, my main source was what I saw and what was happening before my eyes in most cases. I had little or no briefing from Bosnian government, SDA, Muslim authorities. Fairly scant connections with the Red Cross, didn't talk to them much. We disagreed, and they disagreed with me and I with them over their performance in failing to get into and report the camps that we've been discussing. UNHCR some communication, yes. The British Army, some communication, yes, because that's obviously what the newspaper was interested in -- in -- in, our British section of the UNPROFOR. And certainly soldiers, yeah. That I will -- I will grant that most of the military I talked to after the convoy over Vlasic was the -- were -- were the Bosnian Army, not the Mujahedin, who I understood just recently had a contract out on me. They didn't like me at all nor me them, and -- but I would say to the Court, if I may, that I did try to get back into Serbian-held territory after that convoy over Vlasic, which was my first time into the government-held territory apart from 36 hours at Sarajevo airport during the spring, and I was unable to get permission to travel through the Bosnian-held -- sorry, Bosnian Serb-held territory. I made a number of attempts by going to Pale where a member of your family, indeed, and others were vetting and giving licence to some and others not to travel, and I never succeeded in getting official permission. They didn't like me. When I did next go into the Republika Srpska was after the war when I went to Visegrad without authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's -- let me bring this to an end. In the Tadic case, on the 6th of June, 1996, on page 2076 you described the situation, and you said that you monitored official reports by many organisations such as UNHCR, the Red Cross, and so on and so forth. This is 1D04801, and in that transcript, page number is 2075 and also 2076. You have just said a very important thing. You said that you based most of your information on what you saw. Does this mean that you still stand by your first text that we saw today dated the 7th of August, because it says there that you saw things with your own eyes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: On the 7th of August, the article, yes. That's mostly based on our visits on the 5th of August to the camps, and -- yes, of course I saw the reports by these various international organisations. I didn't use them as much as many other people did, nor did I go to their briefings as often as others. Sorry, to clarify the, 7th of August article is based upon what -- in most part upon what I saw in Omarska and Trnopolje that day, 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We have to wrap up, Mr. Karadzic. I think you have concluded, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So there are no other texts based on what you saw, based on your visit, but that one. This is the first text which was written before the media circus descended upon Bosnia; right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. Apart from 36 hours at Sarajevo airport back in April, I had not set foot in -- in Bosnian government controlled territory. I had no other sources apart from what we saw that day in addition to the briefing -- apart from the briefing with you, which I acted upon immediately, as we've discussed, going to Capljina to Dretelj, and -- but I had not been briefed by -- if you're asking me if I'd been briefed by the Bosnian side, I'd seen their lists, but I had not actually set foot in Bosnian government controlled territory apart from Sarajevo airport, which was a demilitarised zone, a UN zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just inform you, Mr. Vulliamy, that the text dated the 7th of August is accepted by every Serb as a piece of journalism, the only piece of journalist -- journalism. The rest is nothing but a big story, and I'm really sorry that you put yourself in such a position, and that you were finally proclaimed an anti-Serb. And that is not on the basis of the text that you authored on the 7th of August, but based on everything else that can be called a big story and was written after the 7th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unnecessary comment. Unless you wish to comment on that, I'll ask the -- ask Ms. Sutherland to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just to say that I have absolutely nothing against the Serbian people whatsoever. I -- my complaint is against things that were done in their name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just quickly, Mr. Vulliamy. At page -- transcript page 81 today, Mr. Karadzic asked you that you saw no single emaciated person like that person Alic was, actually looking at a still on the screen. I wanted to show you some short video footage. Mr. Reid has that ready. If you could just watch this. And this is starting at -- from 65 ter number 40437, and it's at 9:02 to 9:25.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And again at 13:33 to 14:09, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I can be of assistance. I can hear in the background: "Give me all the emaciated ones." You can check that. The cameraman says: "Bring me those emaciated ones." You can rewind and perhaps you can check.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, clearly there are emaciated prisoners -- detainees in the camp, if that's what's being said in the background.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But my question, Mr. Vulliamy, is did you see these men that we've just seen and/or people like it when you were there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: In that compound, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. The second point -- the second topic: On transcript pages 85 and 86 today, just earlier there was discussion about Mrs. Balaban interpreting, and you said that -- you mentioned that Drljaca, Meakic, and Milutinovic were in authority and that Balaban was interpreting for them. When Ian Williams, the ITN reporter, said, "Why aren't you fulfilling Karadzic's promise?" And Mrs. Balaban said, "He said you can see this and this and not that," was that the restrictions on access that you referred to earlier as imposed by Karadzic? Is that what you were talking about when you said there was the bit that mattered? Were you --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- referring --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: That was what --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- to the restrictions on access that were referred to earlier as being imposed by Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: That was one of the passages, and be it coming from her own mouth or translated, I'm not in a position always to know which is -- which is which, when she's translating and when she's just talking, but, yes, that was one of the passages in which it was -- it appeared to be being made clear to her that there were two sets of instructions and that their's was not to allow us into the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But the instructions -- when -- when Ian Williams says, "Why are you not fulfilling Dr. Karadzic's promise to us?" And she said, "He promised us something else and said that you can do this and this and that and not that" --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If they say this is the protocol of your stay, that will be all, that -- that he was -- she was talking about Mr. Karadzic was imposing the restriction?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: That -- [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is that how you understood it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: That was my inference, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honour, and if I can tender the video-clip shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Into two parts?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Or it's already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just one additional question if I may, please, concerning the protocol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I don't think it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to ask the witness whether he ever saw the protocol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No it's for the Chamber to assess it later. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Vulliamy. We didn't allow the accused to put the question. Please don't mind. So on behalf of my colleagues and the Tribunal, I would like to thank you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- for coming to The Hague --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- yet again to give it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Most kind. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most kind. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the witness could be excused. With the indulgence of the staff, I have just one brief administrative matter to deal with before we adjourn today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, it's going back to your brief response on the accused's motion for access to Oric document that relates to the witness Tucker, I think. The Chamber would prefer to get a written response from you by the end of this week indicating as follows: Number one, whether or not you -- the Prosecution opposes the motion in light of the developments you mentioned yesterday and the fact that all documents, save for one, seem to have been disclosed. Number two, whether or not the Prosecution has disclosed any confidential document to the accused already. Number three, if so, on what basis were these disclosed given that the Pre-Trial Chamber ruled that the accused should have -- should not have access to the confidential materials in the Oric case? Number four, if confidential documents were, nevertheless, disclosed, the Chamber would like to know the exact numbers from the Oric case that were disclosed and whether these include Defence exhibits. And number five, finally, with respect to the Rule 70 document that remains outstanding, the Chamber would like to know what that document is as well as its exhibit number in the Oric case. Thank you. Hearing is now adjourned. Tomorrow 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
